choices: CPU utilization measures resource usage, not user experience — a good SLI quantifies what users feel (request success rate, latency percentiles), because the SLO exists to protect users, not servers
70% is too high; the SLO should be < 50% to be safe
Average is wrong; they should use the maximum CPU across the fleet
SLIs must be defined by the infrastructure team, not the service team
scenarios.hint: If this SLI is green but every user request fails, what has the SLO actually protected?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this SLI?
scenarios.situation: A team defines their SLI as 'average CPU utilization across the fleet' with an SLO of '< 70%'.
scenarios.title: Picking a Good SLI
scenarios.why: SLIs must reflect the user's experience of the service: proportion of successful requests, latency of successful requests, freshness of data. Resource metrics are useful for capacity planning and alerting internals, but a service can be at 40% CPU and completely broken (or 95% CPU and perfectly healthy). SLOs on the wrong signal drive the wrong behavior.

choices: Freeze non-urgent feature releases and focus on reliability work until the budget recovers — the error budget is the agreed trade-off mechanism: budget spent means reliability work takes priority over features
Ship anyway; SLOs are aspirational and budgets reset monthly
Lower the SLO to 99% so the budget is no longer exhausted
Exclude the bad deploy's errors from the SLI retroactively
evidence:
Error budget: 43.2 min/month
Consumed by day 10: 43.2 min (100%)
scenarios.hint: The budget is a deal made in advance between product and engineering. What was the deal?
scenarios.prompt: What does the error-budget policy dictate?
scenarios.situation: The checkout service has a 99.9% SLO (43 min/month error budget). It's the 10th and the budget is fully burned after a bad deploy. Product wants to ship a big feature on the 12th.
scenarios.title: Error Budget Exhausted
scenarios.why: The error budget makes the reliability/feature trade-off explicit and pre-negotiated: as long as budget remains, ship fast; when it's gone, reliability work wins. That's the entire point — decisions during calm times, not arguments during incidents. Retroactively editing the SLI or lowering the SLO to dodge the policy destroys trust in the system.

choices: Establish command: declare the incident, assign roles (commander, communications, ops), set a coordination rhythm — parallel uncoordinated debugging wastes the critical first minutes and leaves stakeholders blind
Let the most senior engineer debug alone; too many cooks spoil the incident
Immediately roll back the last deploy; action beats process
Wait 15 minutes to see if monitoring self-resolves before declaring
scenarios.hint: Five people debugging five theories with no updates — what role is missing?
scenarios.prompt: What is the incident commander's first move?
scenarios.situation: The payments API is down. Five engineers are in the incident channel, all debugging different theories, and nobody is updating the status page.
scenarios.title: Incident Commander First Move
scenarios.why: The first minutes of an incident are a coordination problem, not a technical one. Declaring the incident and assigning roles (who debugs, who communicates, who tracks time) converts chaos into parallel productive work and ensures stakeholders get updates. Blind rollback without diagnosis can worsen things; waiting wastes the golden window.

choices: Blame fixes nothing: the system allowed a single command to cause an outage, so the action items must address systemic causes (guardrails, confirmations, dry-run modes, blast-radius limits) — blameless postmortems keep people honest, and honesty is what finds real root causes
The engineer should be named so others learn from the example
'Be more careful' is sufficient; most outages are human error
Skip the postmortem; the cause is obvious
scenarios.hint: If a careful, well-rested engineer could still make this mistake tomorrow, what have you actually fixed by naming them?
scenarios.prompt: Why is this the wrong response, and what should replace it?
scenarios.situation: After an outage caused by an engineer running a destructive command, a manager wants the postmortem to name the engineer and add 'be more careful' as the action item.
scenarios.title: Blameless Postmortem Pushback
scenarios.why: Human error is never the root cause — it's the starting point. If one mistyped command can take down production, the system is fragile by design: missing confirmations, no dry-run, excessive privileges, no canary. Blame drives incidents underground (people hide mistakes), while blameless analysis surfaces the systemic fixes that prevent entire classes of failure.

choices: Cap toil (Google's SRE book sets the bar at 50% max, aiming lower), then systematically automate the toil away — adding headcount to a toil-heavy team just scales the toil linearly instead of eliminating it
Hire two more SREs; toil is normal operations work
Outsource the toil to a managed services vendor and keep headcount flat
Accept 60% toil; SRE is mostly operations anyway
scenarios.hint: If traffic doubles, what happens to this toil — and what happens to it if you automate it instead?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct SRE response before hiring?
scenarios.situation: The SRE team spends 60% of its time on manual toil: hand-running database migrations, manually rotating certs, clicking through cloud consoles to provision. They ask for headcount.
scenarios.title: Toil Audit
scenarios.why: Toil is the work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, and devoid of enduring value — and it scales with service growth, so hiring into it is a treadmill. The SRE discipline: measure toil, cap it, and spend the freed engineering time automating it away. Each automation permanently reduces the toil fraction; each hire without automation just adds capacity for more toil.

choices: Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts (e.g., Google's SRE workbook pattern: fast-burn 1h/5m windows for paging, slow-burn 6h/30m for tickets) tied to the error budget — fast burns page, slow burns ticket, and both reset correctly
Lower the threshold to 0.1% so the slow burn would have paged
Raise the `for:` duration to 1 hour to stop the noisy pages
Alert on total error count instead of ratio; ratios hide slow burns
evidence: 0.4% errors for 6h = budget exhausted, never paged
scenarios.hint: You need two different urgencies: 'budget burning fast, wake someone' and 'budget leaking slowly, file a ticket'. How many thresholds does that need?
scenarios.prompt: What alerting design fixes both failure modes?
scenarios.situation: The team pages on 'error rate > 1% for 5 minutes'. They get paged for brief spikes that self-resolve, and once missed a slow burn that exhausted the budget over 6 hours without ever tripping the alert.
scenarios.title: Multi-Window Burn Alerts
scenarios.why: Single-threshold alerts can't distinguish a 5-minute spike from a 6-hour bleed. Burn-rate alerting ties directly to the SLO: the fast-burn alert catches budget consumption at 14.4x+ (page-worthy), the slow-burn catches 6x+ over long windows (ticket-worthy). Both use paired long/short windows so alerts reset promptly when the burn stops, avoiding flapping.

scenarios.title: The aspirational 99.99%
scenarios.situation: Product demands a 99.99% SLO for the internal admin dashboard 'because reliability matters'. The dashboard is used by 5 admins, business hours only.
evidence: 99.99% SLO for admin dashboard (5 users, business hours)
choices: Negotiate down with data: 4.3 min/month leaves no room for deploys; propose 99.9% (43 min) or 99.5% with a comms SLA — match the SLO to actual user need and cost
Refuse any SLO for internal tools
scenarios.hint: What does 99.99% cost in minutes per month?
scenarios.why: 4.3 minutes per month is unworkable for a normal deploy cadence — the team would spend the budget on routine releases and live in freeze. The SLO should match user need (5 admins, business hours) and cost reality; 99.9% or even 99.5% with a communication SLA serves them fine. Choice 2 pays five-nines cost for no user benefit. Choice 3 is dishonest. Choice 4 swings too far — internal tools deserve SLOs, just appropriate ones. Correct: negotiate with math.

scenarios.title: Toil at 60% and rising
scenarios.situation: The SRE team's toil audit shows 60% of time on manual repetitive work, trending up. Feature teams keep requesting 'just one manual deploy process'.
evidence: toil: 60% of SRE time, +8% per quarter
3 new manual processes requested this month
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct leadership response?
choices: Enforce the toil cap: halt new manual processes (require automation plans), reserve sprint capacity for eliminating the top toil sources, and report the trend upward
Hire more SREs to absorb the toil
Accept it — toil is the job
scenarios.hint: What happens to the trend if you just add people?
scenarios.why: 60% and rising means the team is drowning: more hires (choice 2) scale the toil linearly without fixing it, and 'spare time' (choice 4) doesn't exist at 60% toil. The SRE practice is explicit — cap operational work at 50%, measure toil, and fund elimination from sprint capacity. New manual processes get automation plans or get declined. Correct: enforce the cap and fund elimination.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Sre Practices as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The SRE Practices Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that SRE Practices is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in SRE Practices?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — SRE Practices issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — SRE Practices is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is SRE Practices supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any SRE Practices failure in Sre Practices.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to SRE Practices
evidence: All SRE Practices components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Error Budgets: Policy & Practice
domains.description: Budget math, burn rates, policy enforcement, and budget-driven launch decisions.

scenarios.title: The 7-day window that punished one bad day
scenarios.situation: A team uses a 7-day SLO window. One 30-minute incident consumed 90% of the budget; the team froze for a week over a single event.
choices: Move to a 30-day window: the same incident becomes ~25% of budget — proportionate response instead of a week-long freeze over one event
Keep 7 days but raise the SLO to 99%
scenarios.hint: What fraction of the window did one incident consume?
scenarios.why: A 7-day window makes the budget hypersensitive — one incident dominates the whole period, forcing disproportionate freezes. The 30-day window keeps the same SLO but absorbs single events proportionally; policy still triggers, just sanely. Choice 2 changes the target instead of the window. Choice 3 corrupts the measurement. Choice 4 doubles down on the overreaction. Correct: 30-day window.

scenarios.title: The composed SLO shortfall
scenarios.situation: Checkout promises 99.9% but depends on payments (99.9%), inventory (99.9%), and auth (99.9%) with no fallbacks.
choices: Fix the composition: tighten a dependency SLO, add fallbacks/caching, or lower the checkout SLO to what the math supports — then document the budget contract
scenarios.hint: What does 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 equal?
scenarios.why: The math is inexorable: serial 99.9%s compose to 99.7%. 'Trying harder' (choice 2) doesn't change multiplication. The honest fixes are structural — better deps, fallbacks that break the serial chain, or an SLO the composition can actually meet. Choice 3/4 are denial. Correct: recompose honestly.

scenarios.title: Freeze called too late
scenarios.situation: The budget hit zero on the 12th. The freeze was called on the 25th after two more incidents. Nobody owned the decision.
evidence: no named arbiter; 'we were discussing it'
choices: A named arbiter empowered to call the freeze, with the trigger defined in advance — policy that executes without a meeting
A higher SLO so the budget lasts longer
Blaming the team for the incidents
scenarios.hint: Who was allowed to call the freeze on day 12?
scenarios.why: Thirteen days of discussion while the budget was gone — the policy existed but nobody could execute it. A named arbiter with pre-defined triggers turns 'should we freeze?' from a debate into an action. Choices 2/3 avoid the governance gap. Choice 4 is blame. Correct: executable policy with an owner.

scenarios.title: Launch during thin budget
scenarios.situation: A major launch is scheduled Friday. The error budget is at 15% after a rough month. Product says 'we committed to the date'.
choices: Apply the policy: thin budget → extended canary + SRE review, or delay — the date commitment didn't account for budget state; escalate with the tradeoff explicit
Launch as planned; dates are dates
Launch silently without the canary to save time
scenarios.hint: What is the budget for — if not launch risk?
scenarios.why: 15% budget with 10 days left means almost no room for launch risk — the policy exists for exactly this. Options are proportional: extra validation, delay, or explicit exec acceptance of the risk. Choice 2 ignores the budget entirely. Choice 3 overreacts. Choice 4 removes safety to save time — backwards. Correct: policy-driven decision with the tradeoff escalated explicitly.

scenarios.title: The slow leak nobody paged
scenarios.situation: Error rate crept from 0.05% to 0.4% over three weeks. No alert fired (threshold was 1%). The monthly budget is now 80% consumed with a week left.
choices: Slow-burn alert: multi-day window comparing burn rate to budget — tickets when consumption exceeds the sustainable pace, long before the threshold
scenarios.hint: What would have fired two weeks ago?
scenarios.why: A fixed 1% threshold is blind to gradual leaks — the budget bled out underneath it. Slow-burn alerts watch the rate of budget consumption over days: at 80% consumed with a week left, the pace is clearly unsustainable, and a ticket fires weeks earlier. Choice 2 just moves the blind spot. Choice 3 is noise. Choice 4 relies on humans noticing trends. Correct: burn-rate-based slow alert.

scenarios.title: SLO for a brand-new service
scenarios.situation: A new service launches next month with zero production history. Product wants an SLO in the launch announcement.
choices: Set a provisional SLO from similar services, announce it as provisional, and review after 30 days of real data — then set the real one
Refuse any SLO until 6 months of data
scenarios.hint: What can you know about reliability before any traffic?
scenarios.why: No data means any SLO is a guess — but 'no SLO' means no budget governance during the riskiest period. The provisional SLO (borrowed from similar services, explicitly provisional, reviewed at 30 days) gives the launch budget discipline without false precision. Choice 2 invents a promise. Choice 3 leaves the launch ungoverned. Choice 4 copies without basis. Correct: provisional, then data-driven.

scenarios.title: Budget overdrawn: negative
scenarios.situation: A bad month consumed 130% of the error budget (overdrawn). The team debates whether the freeze still applies — 'the month is over anyway'.
choices: The new window starts fresh, but the overdraw triggers a reliability review: what broke, what changes before the next risky launch — the freeze lifts, the learning doesn't
Fresh start, no review — windows reset everything
Extend the freeze indefinitely as punishment
Lower the SLO so it doesn't happen again
scenarios.hint: What does the overdraw tell you that the new window doesn't erase?
scenarios.why: Rolling windows reset the arithmetic — that's by design. But 130% consumption is a signal demanding a review: systemic causes, action items, and launch caution until they're addressed. Choice 2 wastes the signal. Choice 3 is punitive, not corrective. Choice 4 moves the goalposts instead of fixing the system. Correct: fresh budget, mandatory learning review.

domains.summary: Deep dive on error budgets: the central governance mechanism of SRE.

domains.name: Blameless Culture & Psychological Safety
domains.description: Blamelessness in practice, psychological safety, and learning-oriented reviews.

scenarios.title: The named-and-shamed postmortem
scenarios.situation: A postmortem title reads 'Checkout outage caused by Ana's deploy'. Ana now avoids deploys and stopped speaking in reviews.
evidence: Ana avoids deploys; silent in reviews
choices: Rewrite systemically ('Unvalidated config in deploy pipeline caused checkout outage'), address the pipeline gap, and repair the safety damage — publicly affirm the blameless norm
Tell Ana to be less sensitive
scenarios.hint: What will Ana do the next time she makes a mistake?
scenarios.why: Naming Ana punished honesty: she'll hide the next mistake instead of reporting it, and the pipeline gap (unvalidated config) stays open. The systemic rewrite + the actual fix (validation) + visible leadership reaffirmation of blamelessness repairs both the system and the safety. Choices 2/3 blame the victim. Choice 4 hides the learning. Correct: systemic framing, real fix, safety repair.

scenarios.title: 'Be more careful' action item
scenarios.situation: A postmortem's only action item: 'Engineers will be more careful with config changes.' Three months later, the same class of incident recurs.
scenarios.prompt: Why did it fail, and what's the right action?
choices: 'Be careful' isn't an engineering control — humans err at constant rates; the right action is systemic (config schema validation in CI), which works regardless of carefulness
The action needed a stricter deadline
scenarios.hint: What is the human error rate for careful vs careless engineers?
scenarios.why: 'Be more careful' asks humans to defeat their own error rate by willpower — it never works, which is why the incident recurred. Systemic actions (validation, guardrails, automation) prevent the error class entirely. Choices 2/3 blame harder. Choice 4 surrenders. Correct: replace vigilance with engineering.

scenarios.title: Exec asks 'who caused this?'
scenarios.situation: In the exec review, the CTO asks 'whose fault was this outage?' The room goes quiet.
scenarios.prompt: How should the SRE lead respond?
choices: Translate: 'No individual fault — three systemic gaps allowed it; here are the fixes with owners and dates.' Give leadership rigor, not a scapegoat
Name the engineer to satisfy the CTO
Say 'we don't do blame here' and move on
scenarios.hint: What does the CTO actually need — a name, or assurance it won't recur?
scenarios.why: The CTO wants accountability — which blameless culture provides as systemic fixes with owners and dates, not as a person. Naming someone (choice 2) destroys safety org-wide; the word 'blameless' alone (choice 3) sounds evasive without the rigor behind it. The lead's job is translation: answer the accountability need in systemic language. Correct: systemic causes + owned fixes.

scenarios.title: The intern's unheard warning
scenarios.situation: An intern noticed the risky config in review but didn't speak up ('I'm new'). The incident happened; the intern feels guilty.
evidence: intern saw the risk, stayed silent
intern guilt; team unaware of the dynamic
choices: Treat the silence as the finding: why didn't the intern feel safe speaking? Fix the review dynamic (explicit invitation for concerns, no-rank rule) and tell the intern the system failed them, not vice versa
Reassure the intern it wasn't their job
Require interns to approve risky changes
scenarios.hint: How many other silent observers are in your reviews?
scenarios.why: The incident's deepest cause isn't the config — it's that the person who saw it couldn't speak. 'Not your job' (choice 2) cements the silence. The fix is structural: reviews that explicitly invite dissent, no-rank norms, and leadership visibly valuing the warning. And the intern needs to hear the system failed them. Correct: fix the safety, not the intern.

scenarios.title: Repeat 'honest mistake'
scenarios.situation: The same engineer has caused three similar incidents — each an honest mistake under time pressure, each blamelessly reviewed, each with systemic fixes shipped.
evidence: 3 similar incidents, same engineer, time pressure each time
scenarios.prompt: How does just culture handle this?
choices: Look at the pattern, not the person: repeated time-pressure mistakes signal a systemic load problem — address the pressure (staffing, deadlines), coach the engineer, keep it blameless
It's blameless, so do nothing about the pattern
Punish the engineer — three times is enough
Move the engineer off critical work quietly
scenarios.hint: What is common across all three incidents — the person, or the conditions?
scenarios.why: Three similar incidents under time pressure is data about the system (chronic pressure), not the person. Just culture distinguishes: honest mistakes → system fixes; the pattern here points at load/pressure as the system cause. Coaching + pressure relief is the response. Choice 2 ignores the pattern. Choice 3 punishes someone the system set up. Choice 4 is quiet blame. Correct: address the systemic pressure.

scenarios.title: Blameless in customer comms
scenarios.situation: A status page draft reads: 'An engineer mistakenly deleted the production database.' Legal wants it published as-is for 'transparency'.
choices: Systemic and customer-focused: 'A database maintenance operation affected production; we've restored service and added safeguards...' — customers need impact and fix, not a scapegoat
scenarios.hint: What does the customer need to decide or do with this information?
scenarios.why: Customers need to know impact, current status, and prevention — naming the engineer serves none of those and destroys internal safety (every engineer now fears the status page). Transparency is about the system cause and the fix, not the person. Choice 3 withholds useful cause info. Correct: systemic cause, impact, safeguards — no names.

scenarios.title: Measuring safety
scenarios.situation: Leadership claims 'we have a blameless culture' but postmortems are thin and nobody volunteers mistakes.
scenarios.prompt: How do you test the claim?
choices: Measure it: anonymous safety pulse surveys plus behavioral signals (junior speak-up rate, volunteered mistakes, dissent in reviews) — then act on the gap
Accept the claim; culture is intangible
scenarios.hint: What would prove the claim true?
scenarios.why: The gap between claim and behavior is the finding — and it needs data, not assertion. Pulse surveys + behavioral signals make safety discussable and trackable; acting on the results (facilitator training, leadership modeling) closes the gap. Choice 2 surrenders to vagueness. Choice 3 without measurement is theater. Choice 4 is too slow to steer by. Correct: measure, then act.

domains.summary: The cultural foundation: blamelessness and psychological safety.

domains.name: Postmortems That Change Things
domains.description: Writing effective postmortems, action items, and follow-through discipline.

scenarios.title: Postmortem from memory, three weeks late
scenarios.situation: A SEV1 postmortem was written 3 weeks later from memory. Two engineers disagree on the timeline; the 'root cause' is disputed.
choices: Postmortem within days, timeline built from logs/chat/tool timestamps — not memory; assign the facilitator at incident close
Let the IC write it alone
scenarios.hint: What evidence exists at day 2 that doesn't at day 21?
scenarios.why: Memory compresses and self-serves; three weeks later the facts are gone and the review becomes narrative wars. The practice: facilitator assigned at incident close, draft timeline from timestamps within 48h, review within 5 days. Choices 2/3 don't fix the evidence problem. Choice 4 guarantees repeat incidents. Correct: fast, evidence-based, facilitated.

scenarios.title: The single root cause
scenarios.situation: A postmortem names 'the root cause: DNS failure'. Action item: 'fix DNS'. Six months later a similar outage occurs via a different path.
scenarios.prompt: What was wrong with the analysis?
choices: Single-cause thinking: the outage needed DNS failure AND missing fallback AND no drill AND slow detection — fixing one factor leaves the others; list contributing factors and address the set
The action item needed an earlier deadline
scenarios.hint: What else had to be true for the DNS failure to become an outage?
scenarios.why: Outages are never monocausal — they require the alignment of multiple factors. 'Fix DNS' addressed one; the missing fallback, undrilled playbook, and slow detection remained, so a different trigger walked the same path. The practice: enumerate contributing factors and action the set. Correct: plural causes, plural fixes.

scenarios.title: Vague action items die
scenarios.situation: Last quarter's postmortems produced 24 action items like 'improve monitoring' and 'review process'. 3 are done.
choices: Action-item discipline: single owner + due date + definition of done for each ('Add burn-rate alert with runbook by Fri — done = alert fires in staging test'), tracked on a visible board, reviewed weekly
Assign all items to the SRE team
scenarios.hint: What makes 'add burn-rate alert by Friday' different from 'improve monitoring'?
scenarios.why: 'Improve monitoring' has no owner, no date, no done-criteria — it's a wish, and wishes don't ship. The discipline (owner + date + done-definition + visible tracking + weekly review) converts wishes into work. Choices 2/3 reduce the practice. Choice 4 overloads one team. Correct: specific, owned, tracked.

scenarios.title: Repeat causes keep recurring
scenarios.situation: Three postmortems in a year cite 'config change without validation'. Each had an action item; each was marked done differently.
choices: Treat recurrence as the finding: audit whether the actions actually addressed the cause class (they didn't — three different partial fixes); implement the class-level fix (config validation in CI for all services) and track repeat-cause rate as a practice metric
Write a fourth postmortem the same way
scenarios.hint: What do three 'done' actions and a fourth incident prove?
scenarios.why: Recurrence proves the actions didn't work — three partial fixes, same cause class. The practice-level response: measure repeat-cause rate, and fix the class (org-wide config validation), not the instance. Choice 2 repeats the failure. Choice 3 is blame. Choice 4 surrenders. Correct: class-level fix + repeat-cause metric.

scenarios.title: Protagonist facilitates own incident
scenarios.situation: The engineer whose deploy caused the outage facilitated the postmortem. The review was defensive; contributing factors from their area went unexplored.
choices: A neutral facilitator: not the protagonist, not their manager — someone who can ask naive questions and redirect defensiveness without hierarchy in the room
Let the protagonist facilitate; they know the most
Have the manager facilitate for authority
scenarios.hint: Who can ask 'why did you do that?' without it sounding like an accusation?
scenarios.why: The protagonist can't neutrally probe their own decisions — defensiveness is human, and the room follows their lead into soft-pedaling. Neutral facilitation (peer from another team, trained) creates the safety to examine everything. Choice 2 caused this. Choice 3 loses the human skill. Choice 4 adds hierarchy, chilling honesty. Correct: neutral, trained facilitator.

scenarios.title: Only what went wrong
scenarios.situation: Postmortems list only failures. The team is demoralized; the brilliant 10-minute mitigation gets no mention.
choices: 'What went well' as a required section: name the effective detection, the fast mitigation, the good comms — reinforce the practices that worked so they repeat
scenarios.hint: How does the team learn to repeat the 10-minute mitigation?
scenarios.why: Postmortems that only catalog failure teach 'incidents = punishment' and let good practices go unrecognized (and unrepeated). Naming what worked — the alert that fired fast, the runbook that nailed it — reinforces the behaviors you want more of. Choices 2/4 dodge the learning. Choice 3 inverts the bias. Correct: balanced review, both sections required.

scenarios.title: Private postmortems
scenarios.situation: Postmortems are restricted to the owning team 'to avoid embarrassment'. Other teams keep hitting the same failure modes.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right sharing model?
choices: Publish postmortems org-wide (sanitized as needed): other teams learn without paying the incident cost — the multiplier effect is the point
scenarios.hint: How many teams should pay for one team's incident?
scenarios.why: Team-only postmortems privatize the learning while the failure mode stays public — three teams paid for the same lesson. Sanitized org-wide publishing multiplies every incident's value. 'Embarrassment' (choice 2) is exactly what blameless culture addresses. Choice 3 strips the context that teaches. Correct: default to shared.

scenarios.title: Skipping the 'minor' postmortem
scenarios.situation: A SEV3 (brief latency spike, auto-recovered) got no postmortem. Two months later the same pattern caused a SEV1.
choices: Review interesting SEV3s lightweightly: the auto-recovery masked a real weakness; a 30-minute review then would have found what the SEV1 later proved
More auto-recovery so SEV3s don't matter
scenarios.hint: What did the auto-recovery hide?
scenarios.why: SEV3s are free lessons — the system showed you a weakness at low cost. Auto-recovery isn't a fix; it's a mask. A lightweight review (30 min, timeline, one or two actions) harvests the learning before the pattern scales up. Choice 2 guarantees the SEV1 surprise. Choice 3 trusts the mask. Correct: review the interesting small ones.

domains.summary: Postmortems as the learning engine: structure, action items, follow-through.

domains.name: Toil Elimination
domains.description: Identifying toil, toil budgets, automation strategy, and self-service.

scenarios.title: Toil by anecdote
scenarios.situation: The team 'feels' toil is high but has no numbers. Prioritization debates go in circles; automation never gets funded.
choices: A toil audit with numbers: sample on-call weeks, classify tasks, total toil hours, rank sources by frequency × pain — data funds automation
scenarios.hint: What convinces a roadmap meeting — feelings or numbers?
scenarios.why: Anecdotes lose to feature work every time; numbers compete. The audit converts 'we feel busy' into '38% of on-call is toil, here are the top 3 sources' — a fundable proposal. Choice 2 automates by volume of complaint, not ROI. Choice 3 institutionalizes toil. Choice 4 waits for burnout. Correct: measure, then fund.

scenarios.title: Automating the wrong thing
scenarios.situation: The team automated certificate renewals (2/year, 30 min each) while manual deploys (34/month, 2h each, error-prone) continue by hand.
choices: No ROI ordering: automation priority = frequency × pain × error rate. Certs felt automatable; deploys were the actual bleed
scenarios.hint: Compare the yearly hours: 1 vs 816.
scenarios.why: They automated what was easy, not what mattered — 1 hour/year saved while 816 hours/year bleed. ROI ordering (frequency × pain × error-rate) would have ranked manual deploys first by orders of magnitude. Choice 2 is wrong — the cert work was fine, just mis-prioritized. Correct: prioritize by ROI.

scenarios.title: The script nobody trusts
scenarios.situation: An engineer scripted the deploy toil, but it has no dry-run, no logging, and failed halfway twice. The team went back to manual deploys.
evidence: no dry-run, no logs, 2 partial failures
choices: Production discipline: idempotent, dry-run mode, logging, monitoring, tested rollback — automation must be more reliable than the toil it replaces
Force the team to use it
scenarios.hint: Why did the team rationally go back to manual?
scenarios.why: A flaky script is worse than toil — it adds incidents to the manual work. The team rationally reverted. Automation earns trust through production discipline: idempotency, dry-run, logs, monitoring, rollback. Choices 2/3 add pressure without reliability. Choice 4 wastes the investment. Correct: make it trustworthy, then re-adopt.

scenarios.title: Manual path kept 'just in case'
scenarios.situation: Deploy automation works, but the manual runbook is still maintained 'just in case'. Both paths drift; new hires learn the manual one.
evidence: automation works; manual path maintained in parallel
runbook outdated; hires learn manual first
scenarios.prompt: What is the actual toil reduction?
choices: Zero — maintaining two paths is more work than one, and the team defaults to the manual path under pressure. Delete the manual path (keep an escape hatch in the automation)
scenarios.hint: Which path does the team use at 3am — and why?
scenarios.why: Two maintained paths = more toil than one, plus the team backslides to manual under pressure (it's the 'known' path). Real toil elimination deletes the manual path — with the escape hatch built into the automation (dry-run, manual override flags), not as a parallel universe. Correct: delete, don't duplicate.

scenarios.title: Ticket-queue toil
scenarios.situation: The platform team gets 400 tickets/quarter: 'provision env', 'bump quota', 'rotate secret'. Engineers spend 30% of time on tickets.
choices: Self-service for the top 3 ticket types with guardrails: provision button, auto-approve quota under limits, one-click rotation — deflect 75% of tickets
scenarios.hint: What fraction of tickets do the top 3 types represent?
scenarios.why: The top 3 types are 75% of volume — three self-service automations with guardrails eliminate the bulk permanently. Triage staff (choice 2) scales the toil. Faster SLAs (choice 3) optimize the queue instead of shrinking it. Templates (choice 4) polish the toil. Correct: self-service the head of the distribution.

scenarios.title: New manual process request
scenarios.situation: A product team requests a new manual deploy-approval process: 'just have SRE click approve on each deploy'.
choices: Decline the manual version; offer the automated equivalent (policy checks in CI auto-approve standard deploys, flag the risky ones) — new toil needs an automation plan or a no
scenarios.hint: What is 'one click' × 50/week × forever?
scenarios.why: 'Just one click' × 50/week = permanent toil with an on-call dependency. The SRE response: automate the policy (CI checks encode the approval rules; only exceptions need humans) or decline. Accepting (choices 2/3) grows toil; escalating (choice 4) avoids the engineering answer. Correct: automated policy or no.

scenarios.title: Sprint capacity for toil
scenarios.situation: Toil automation loses to feature work every sprint. 'We'll automate when there's time' — there never is.
choices: Reserve capacity: 15-20% of every sprint for toil automation and postmortem actions — protected like any other commitment, not leftover time
A dedicated 'toil quarter' once a year
Ask engineers to automate on weekends
scenarios.hint: What has higher status in sprint planning — features or 'when there's time'?
scenarios.why: Leftover-time automation never happens — features always fill the vacuum. Reserved capacity makes elimination a commitment with the same status as feature work. The annual quarter (choice 2) lets toil compound for 9 months. Choice 3 burns people out. Correct: protected sprint capacity, every sprint.

scenarios.title: Toil notes lost between rotations
scenarios.situation: Every rotation rediscovers the same flaky alert and the same manual workaround. Knowledge evaporates at handoff.
choices: Handoff includes toil notes as a required section: flaky alerts, manual workarounds, automation ideas — written, and each becomes backlog fuel
Page the previous on-call with questions
scenarios.hint: Where does the workaround live between rotations?
scenarios.why: Verbal handoffs evaporate; the same toil gets rediscovered forever. A required toil-notes section makes the workaround visible once, then converts it to backlog ('flaky alert X paged 4x → tune it'). Choices 2/4 keep it verbal. Correct: written toil notes feeding the automation backlog.

domains.summary: Systematically eliminating toil: measurement, prioritization, automation.

domains.name: SRE, DevOps & Platform: Org Models
domains.description: SRE vs DevOps vs platform engineering, team topologies, embedding models.

scenarios.title: Rebrand without practices
scenarios.situation: The ops team was renamed 'SRE' last quarter. Nothing else changed: no SLOs, no error budgets, ticket-queue work continues.
choices: It's ops with a new title: SRE is defined by practices (SLOs, budgets, toil elimination, blameless postmortems) — adopt the practices or drop the name
The rebrand is complete; SRE achieved
Hire a consultant to bless it
scenarios.hint: Which SRE practices does the team actually do?
scenarios.why: Titles don't create practices. The checklist test (SLOs? budgets? toil measured? blameless postmortems? code written?) fails on every item — this is a rebrand, not a transformation. Choice 2 declares victory over a name change. Choice 3 is half-true: titles don't matter, but practices do. Correct: adopt practices or stop claiming the name.

scenarios.title: Central SRE as ticket queue
scenarios.situation: The central SRE team spends 80% of time on product-team tickets: 'set up monitoring for us', 'tune our alerts', 'run our deploy'.
choices: Shift from ticket-queue to engagement model: time-boxed partnerships that bootstrap the product team's own practices, then hand back — SRE enables, not staffs
Hire more central SREs for the tickets
scenarios.hint: Are product teams more self-sufficient than last year?
scenarios.why: Ticket-queue SRE is staff-augmentation ops: it scales linearly with demand and never builds the product teams' capability. The engagement model (assess → bootstrap → hand back, with exit criteria) transfers practices instead of absorbing work. Choice 2 scales the anti-pattern. Choice 3 monetizes it. Choice 4 abandons the teams. Correct: engagements, not tickets.

scenarios.title: Embedded SRE absorbed
scenarios.situation: Embedded SREs now spend 90% of time on feature work. 'The team needed velocity.' Reliability practices have stalled.
choices: Explicit allocation guardrails: e.g., 50% SRE practices minimum, reviewed quarterly with the SRE org — embedding without guardrails is just reassignment
Pull all SREs back to central
scenarios.hint: What was the SRE hired to do — and what are they doing?
scenarios.why: Embedding without guardrails dissolves the role: the product team's incentives (features now) always beat reliability work later. The fix is structural — contracted practice time, reviewed with the SRE org that owns the mandate. Choice 2 abandons embedding's benefits (context). Choice 3 surrenders the practices. Choice 4 multiplies the absorption. Correct: guardrailed embedding.

scenarios.title: SRE as deploy police
scenarios.situation: SRE must approve every production deploy. The queue is 2 days; teams deploy Friday night to 'beat the queue'. Reliability hasn't improved.
evidence: Friday-night deploys to beat the queue
choices: Replace gates with guardrails: automated policy checks in CI, paved-road deploys, error budgets governing risk — SRE enables safe velocity instead of rationing it
scenarios.hint: What behaviors does the 2-day queue incentivize?
scenarios.why: Manual gates create the exact behaviors they fear: queue-beating, batching, Friday deploys. Guardrails (automated checks, golden paths, budget governance) give safety at velocity — the SRE way. Choices 2/3 scale the gate. Choice 4 treats a symptom. Correct: enable, don't gate.

scenarios.title: SRE ladder to nowhere
scenarios.situation: Senior SREs keep transferring to product teams: 'no Staff path in SRE'. The SRE org is all junior-mid, losing its best automators.
evidence: 3 senior SREs → product teams in a year
SRE caps at Senior; product goes to Principal+
choices: Build a real SRE ladder to Staff/Principal with scope defined in reliability terms (org-wide practices, platform leverage) — or keep losing automators
Pay SREs more at the same level
Tell them SRE is a calling
scenarios.hint: Where can an ambitious SRE grow here?
scenarios.why: People follow growth: a capped ladder exports your best reliability engineers to feature work. The fix is structural — Staff+ scope defined as reliability leverage (practices adopted org-wide, toil eliminated at scale), not as 'senior ticket handler'. Choice 2 helps retention marginally. Choice 3 is insulting. Choice 4 is a treadmill. Correct: real ladder, real scope.

scenarios.title: Choosing the topology
scenarios.situation: A 300-engineer company debates SRE org design: embedded, centralized, or federated. Each faction cites a different tech giant.
evidence: each faction cites a different company
choices: Decide from constraints, not imitation: 300 engineers/40 services → federated (central standards + embedded practitioners) with engagement discipline; validate against toil and SLO coverage, not logos
scenarios.hint: What breaks at 300 engineers under each model?
scenarios.why: Topology follows context: at 300 engineers, pure embedded diverges and pure centralized queues — federated balances both, but only with real engagement discipline. Copying (choice 2) imports someone else's constraints. Choice 3 guarantees divergence. Choice 4 is paralysis. Correct: constraints-driven choice, validated by practice metrics.

scenarios.title: 'We do DevOps, we don't need SRE'
scenarios.situation: Leadership: 'We do DevOps — shared ownership, automation. SRE is just Google's word for it.' No SLOs exist; incidents recur.
evidence: no SLOs, no budgets, recurring incidents
choices: They're complementary: DevOps is the culture, SRE adds the specific practices (SLOs, error budgets, toil caps, blameless postmortems) that turn culture into reliability — adopt the practices, keep the name debate aside
DevOps vs SRE debate until resolved
scenarios.hint: What specifically turns 'shared ownership' into reliability?
scenarios.why: DevOps culture without SRE practices is 'you build it, you run it' with no definition of 'run it well' — hence recurring incidents. SRE supplies the missing machinery: measurable targets, budget governance, toil discipline. It's not either/or. Choice 2 accepts the gap. Choice 3 chases the label. Choice 4 is bikeshedding. Correct: add the practices to the culture.

domains.summary: Organizational models: SRE vs DevOps vs platform, team topologies.

domains.name: Sustainable On-Call
domains.description: On-call health, alert fatigue, compensation, rotations, and burnout prevention.

scenarios.title: 12 pages a night
scenarios.situation: The primary gets paged 12 times per night, mostly flaky alerts. The engineer is exhausted; response quality is dropping.
choices: Treat it as a reliability emergency: immediate alert-quality sprint (tune/delete noisy alerts, add runbooks), page-budget enforcement, and recovery time for the engineer — fatigue is a safety issue
Tell the engineer to toughen up
scenarios.hint: What happens on the 13th page — the real one?
scenarios.why: 12 pages/night of noise will cause the miss that matters — fatigue degrades the exact judgment incidents need. This is a defect backlog (noisy alerts), not a staffing problem: tune/delete, enforce page budgets, give recovery. Choice 2 spreads the damage. Choice 3 is abusive. Choice 4 adds cost without fixing the noise. Correct: fix the alerts, protect the human.

scenarios.title: Two-person rotation, indefinitely
scenarios.situation: Two engineers rotate on-call weekly, indefinitely. Both are interviewing elsewhere; 'we'll hire soon' has been said for 8 months.
choices: Acknowledge the emergency: merge rotations with a neighboring team or pay for external coverage immediately, and make hiring the top priority — a 2-person indefinite rotation is a burnout guarantee
scenarios.hint: What is the recovery time in a 2-person weekly rotation?
scenarios.why: A 2-person rotation means on-call every other week forever — no recovery, no resilience to illness or vacation. 'Hiring soon' for 8 months is not a plan. The immediate fix is structural (merge rotations, buy coverage); the durable fix is hiring as the actual top priority. Choices 2/3/4 nibble at a burnout guarantee. Correct: emergency coverage + real hiring priority.

scenarios.title: Uncompensated on-call
scenarios.situation: On-call is 'part of the job' — no pay differential, no time off after bad nights. Morale is low; volunteers have dried up.
choices: Explicit compensation: on-call pay and/or guaranteed recovery time after disrupted nights, documented — uncompensated on-call taxes trust and retention
It's salaried work; no extra comp needed
Make on-call mandatory for everyone equally
scenarios.hint: What does a 3am page cost the responder?
scenarios.why: Night pages cost sleep and weekends — uncompensated, that's a trust tax that compounds into attrition. Explicit comp (pay, time-off, or both) recognizes the real cost and is table stakes for sustainable on-call. Choices 2/3 dismiss the cost. Choice 4 spreads the resentment. Correct: compensate explicitly.

scenarios.title: Afraid to escalate
scenarios.situation: A junior on-call sat on a growing SEV2 for 90 minutes, afraid to wake the secondary. It became a SEV1.
choices: Normalize early escalation explicitly: 'escalating early is praised, late escalation is the failure' — said by leadership, repeated in reviews, modeled by seniors
Better training so juniors don't need escalation
scenarios.hint: What did the junior believe escalation would signal?
scenarios.why: The junior made a rational choice under a culture where escalation = failure. Training (choice 2) doesn't fix fear; auto-escalation (choice 3) is a fine backstop but doesn't build judgment; seniors-only (choice 4) doesn't scale. The fix is cultural and explicit: leadership states and rewards early escalation until it's the norm. Correct: make escalation safe and praised.

scenarios.title: First solo shift at 3am
scenarios.situation: A new hire's first on-call shift is solo, overnight, in week 2. They're terrified; the team is 'too busy' to shadow.
choices: Shadow rotations: 2-4 weeks shadowing, then supervised day shifts, then solo — with runbooks and escalation paths reviewed before the first shift
scenarios.hint: How does anyone learn incident judgment safely?
scenarios.why: Solo overnight in week 2 is how you get panic, mistakes, and attrition. Shadowing builds judgment safely: observe, then supervised days, then solo — with the runbooks and escalation paths as the safety net. Choice 2 is hazing. Choice 3 still strands them. Choice 4 delays without preparing. Correct: graduated, supervised onboarding.

scenarios.title: No recovery after the bad week
scenarios.situation: An engineer worked a 60-hour incident week. Monday: normal sprint, full load. 'Thanks for the great work!'
choices: Real recovery: light duties the following week, time off encouraged, sprint commitments adjusted — recovery is operational, not just gratitude
scenarios.hint: What is the engineer's decision quality on Monday?
scenarios.why: Gratitude without recovery is how brutal weeks become resignations. The body and judgment need downtime after sustained incident load — light duties, adjusted commitments, real time off. Choices 2/3/4 treat recovery as optional. It's operational: exhausted engineers make worse decisions next incident. Correct: structured recovery.

scenarios.title: No human metrics
scenarios.situation: Leadership tracks MTTR and uptime but nothing about the on-call humans. Attrition in the SRE org is 35%.
choices: Human-system metrics: pages per shift, sleep interruptions, on-call NPS, time-to-recovery after night pages — reviewed with leadership like any reliability input
scenarios.hint: What fails first — the dashboards or the people watching them?
scenarios.why: 35% attrition is the system screaming: the humans are failing, which means reliability is failing soon after. Pages/shift, sleep disruption, on-call NPS are leading indicators — MTTR is a lagging one. Reviewing them with leadership makes human sustainability a managed input, not an HR surprise. Correct: measure the humans.

domains.summary: Making on-call sustainable: health, fairness, alert quality.

domains.name: Launch Readiness Reviews
domains.description: Production readiness reviews, launch checklists, and error-budget-aware launches.

scenarios.title: Launch with no readiness review
scenarios.situation: A team launched a new payment service with no readiness review. Day 2: no dashboards, alerts unconfigured, rollback untested — then an incident.
evidence: no dashboards, no alerts, untested rollback
choices: A production readiness review gating the launch: SLOs, dashboards, burn-rate alerts with runbooks, tested rollback, capacity plan — the checklist exists so day-2 isn't a surprise
scenarios.hint: Which checklist would have caught all three gaps?
scenarios.why: Every gap (dashboards, alerts, rollback) is a readiness-checklist item — the review exists to catch exactly this before users do. Choices 2/3/4 don't add the gate. The review is collaborative, not punitive: SRE + team walk the checklist, findings become blockers or accepted risks. Correct: readiness review as a launch gate.

scenarios.title: No go/no-go criteria
scenarios.situation: Launch day: the canary shows elevated errors, but nobody defined 'too elevated'. The team argues for 40 minutes, then ships anyway. Incident follows.
choices: Pre-defined go/no-go criteria: error budget thresholds, canary pass/fail numbers, rollback triggers — decided calmly before launch, executed without debate during
scenarios.hint: When should 'too elevated' have been defined?
scenarios.why: Deciding thresholds mid-launch under pressure goes badly — optimism wins arguments. Pre-defined criteria (canary fails if errors exceed X) make the call automatic and blameless. Choices 2/4 don't remove the ambiguity. Choice 3 without criteria just prolongs it. Correct: criteria before launch day.

scenarios.title: Deploy equals done
scenarios.situation: A major launch deployed Friday at 6pm. The team left for the weekend. Saturday's slow-burn issue became Sunday's SEV1.
choices: Hypercare: the owning team watches closely for 1-2 weeks post-launch with explicit monitoring, on-call awareness, and a fast rollback path — launches don't end at deploy
scenarios.hint: When does a launch's risk actually end?
scenarios.why: The launch's risk window extends well past deploy — slow-burns surface over days. Hypercare (heightened monitoring, team attention, ready rollback for 1-2 weeks) covers it. Choice 2 avoids Fridays but not the window. Choice 3 helps but can't catch everything. Choice 4 is overbroad. Correct: defined hypercare period.

scenarios.title: Flagless risky launch
scenarios.situation: A new pricing engine launched to 100% with no flag and no gradual rollout. The bug affected all checkouts for 25 minutes until rollback completed.
scenarios.prompt: What should the launch have included?
choices: Flag-gated gradual rollout: 1% → 10% → 100% with a kill switch — mitigation in seconds, blast radius bounded during validation
scenarios.hint: How long should 'turn off the new pricing' take?
scenarios.why: The 25-minute mitigation was the failure: a kill switch turns it into seconds, and gradual rollout bounds the initial blast radius to 1%. Choices 2/4 reduce probability, not mitigation time. Choice 3 helps but rollback will always trail a flag flip. Correct: flags + gradual ramp as the default for risky launches.

scenarios.title: Breaking schema change at launch
scenarios.situation: A launch included a column rename in the same deploy. During the rolling deploy, old instances crashed querying the dropped column.
evidence: column rename + code in one deploy
choices: Expand/contract: add new column → dual-write deploy → backfill → switch reads → drop old — each step independently safe and reversible
scenarios.hint: Which code versions are live when the column disappears?
scenarios.why: The crash is structural: rolling deploys guarantee old+new code coexist, so the schema must serve both. Expand/contract sequences it safely; each phase is reversible alone. Choice 2 shortens the crash window. Choice 3 is sometimes fine but unnecessary here. Choice 4 retries the same mistake. Correct: expand/contract.

scenarios.title: Checklist rot
scenarios.situation: The readiness checklist is 4 years old: it references a retired deploy system and misses feature flags entirely. Teams pencil-whip it.
choices: Treat the checklist as a living document: review after launches and incidents, add items for recurring surprise types, remove the obsolete — owned by SRE, versioned
scenarios.hint: What should a recurring launch surprise become?
scenarios.why: A stale checklist teaches teams that the review is theater — pencil-whipping follows. The practice: evolve it from launch reviews and postmortems (recurring surprise → new item), prune the obsolete, keep it minimal. Choices 2/3 worsen the theater. Correct: living checklist, owned and versioned.

scenarios.title: Perfection before launch
scenarios.situation: A new service's launch is blocked 3 months because 'readiness isn't perfect': SLOs need 6 months of data, chaos program 'should be ready first'.
choices: Provisional approval: launch with baseline readiness (SLOs provisional, alerts + runbooks, rollback tested) and a 30-day review — perfection before launch is the enemy of learning
scenarios.hint: What is readiness for — perfection or managed risk?
scenarios.why: Readiness is risk management, not perfection: baseline practices (provisional SLOs, alerts, runbooks, tested rollback) plus a 30-day review gets the service live and learning. Blocking for perfect SLO data (choice 2) costs quarters. Skipping (choice 3) costs incidents. Correct: provisional launch, scheduled review.

domains.summary: Launch readiness: production readiness reviews and safe launches.

domains.name: Disaster Recovery Practice
domains.description: DR planning methodology, backup/restore testing, RTO/RPO from the SRE view.

scenarios.title: The untested failover
scenarios.situation: The DR plan says 'fail over to us-west'. It has never been tested. During a real region outage, the runbook's third step references a decommissioned system.
evidence: real outage; runbook failed at step 3
choices: Quarterly failover drills in production (Tier 0): execute the actual runbook, score RTO/RPO achieved, fix what breaks — untested plans are fiction
scenarios.hint: What is an untested plan worth during an outage?
scenarios.why: Writing isn't testing: only execution reveals the dead references, the missing credentials, the 22-minute DNS surprise. Quarterly production drills (with scorecards and action items) keep the plan real. Choices 2/3 improve the fiction. Choice 4 doubles the untested surface. Correct: drill it for real.

scenarios.title: Backups nobody restored
scenarios.situation: 'Backups succeed nightly' — but the last restore test was 2 years ago, and it failed (missing credentials). Nobody followed up.
choices: Automated monthly restore tests: provision fresh, restore from backup, run smoke tests, report RTO achieved — 'backup succeeded' is not 'we can recover'
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between 'backed up' and 'recoverable'?
scenarios.why: The industry's most repeated lesson: backups are worthless, restores are everything. The failed test 2 years ago was the warning; ignoring it was the failure. Automated monthly restores (timed, smoke-tested, reported) make recovery a proven property. Choices 2/3/4 optimize the unproven. Correct: test the restore.

scenarios.title: Flat DR for everything
scenarios.situation: The wiki, the staging env, and checkout all get active-active DR. DR spend is 3x primary; the wiki team never asked for it.
choices: Tiered DR from signed-off RTO/RPO: Tier 0 (checkout) gets the expensive design; Tier 2 (wiki) gets backups — cost matched to requirement
Uniform DR is simpler; keep it
scenarios.hint: What RTO does the wiki need — in writing?
scenarios.why: Flat gold-plating burns 3x spend where days-long RTO is fine. Tiers convert one impossible requirement into affordable designs per tier, each justified by written numbers. Choice 2/4 defend the waste. Choice 3 decides without the analysis. Correct: tier from requirements.

scenarios.title: Failback surprise
scenarios.situation: Failover to us-west worked. Failing back corrupted data: replication was one-directional and nobody re-synced before returning traffic.
choices: The full cycle: failover AND failback — re-establish replication in reverse, verify sync, then shift traffic. Failback is a second failover, not an undo
scenarios.hint: What happened to us-west's writes during the outage?
scenarios.why: During the outage us-west accumulated writes; returning without re-sync discards them. The drill must cover the full cycle — over, back, verified — because failback has its own failure modes. Choice 2 abandons the primary. Choice 3 speeds up data loss. Choice 4 adds conflict complexity for a drill problem. Correct: drill the round trip.

scenarios.title: Undrilled dependency
scenarios.situation: Your failover worked — but the payments dependency's DR wasn't tested, and it stayed down. Checkout stayed down with it.
choices: Map and drill dependencies: your DR is only as good as your least-drilled dependency — include critical deps in drills or build fallbacks
Your DR was fine; not your problem
scenarios.hint: What does your region serve without payments?
scenarios.why: Clean failover into a down dependency is still an outage. DR planning must map critical dependencies, verify their DR status, and either include them in drills or build fallbacks (cached auth, degraded mode). Choices 2/4 are boundary-drawing, not reliability. Correct: drill the dependency chain.

scenarios.title: Disaster comms improvised
scenarios.situation: During a 6-hour regional outage, customer updates were improvised, contradictory, and 2 hours apart. Twitter filled the gap.
choices: A disaster comms plan: pre-written templates, named spokespeople, 30-min update cadence, separate channels — exercised in drills
scenarios.hint: What decisions shouldn't be made during the disaster?
scenarios.why: Improvised comms under disaster pressure produce contradiction and silence — and the information vacuum fills with speculation. Pre-written templates, designated voices, and drilled cadence remove decisions from the disaster. Choices 2/4 don't fix the process. Choice 3 guarantees the Twitter problem. Correct: planned, templated, drilled comms.

scenarios.title: Missed RTO, no action
scenarios.situation: The drill achieved 45-min RTO against a 15-min target. The report said 'good effort'. No action items were filed.
choices: Treat the miss like an SLO breach: root-cause the 30-min gap (what consumed it?), file P0 action items, re-drill — targets without consequences are wishes
'Good effort' is fine; drills are practice
Drill less often to avoid embarrassment
scenarios.hint: What would happen if an SLO breach got 'good effort' and no actions?
scenarios.why: 'Good effort' without actions guarantees the next real outage also takes 45 minutes. RTO/RPO are SLOs for disaster: misses get root-caused, actioned, and re-drilled. Choice 3 moves the goalposts without analysis (sometimes right, but only after understanding the gap). Choice 4 hides the problem. Correct: breach discipline for DR targets.

domains.summary: Disaster recovery as practiced: planning, testing, RTO/RPO discipline.

domains.name: Service Ownership & Runbooks
domains.description: Ownership models, service handbooks, runbook culture, and operational maturity.

scenarios.title: The orphaned service
scenarios.situation: A critical billing service has no owning team: the authors left, two teams disclaim it, and its alerts page a rotation nobody staffs.
choices: Assign exactly one owning team (with the pager, runbooks, and SLO mandate), backfill the handbook, and audit the catalog for other orphans
scenarios.hint: Who gets paged tonight — specifically?
scenarios.why: Orphaned critical services are incidents waiting: nobody tunes the alerts, nobody owns the SLO, nobody decommissions it. Exactly one owner (never shared — shared = none), plus handbook backfill and a catalog audit for siblings. Choice 2 recreates the problem. Choice 3 trusts luck. Choice 4 is a huge cost for an ownership problem. Correct: single owner + audit.

scenarios.title: 3am with no handbook
scenarios.situation: A new on-call faces an unfamiliar service's incident. No handbook exists; the knowledge is in one senior's head — who's on vacation.
choices: Handbooks as a launch requirement: architecture, SLOs, dashboards, runbooks, known issues — templated org-wide, reviewed quarterly
scenarios.hint: Where should the senior's knowledge live?
scenarios.why: Tribal knowledge fails exactly when needed (vacations, attrition, 3am). The handbook is the on-call's brain: templated, required at launch, kept current by review. Choices 2/4 are expensive and incomplete. Choice 3 is illegal in most places and absurd everywhere. Correct: handbook as launch gate.

scenarios.title: Build team vs run team
scenarios.situation: Feature teams build services; a separate ops team runs them. The builders optimize for ship speed; the runners drown in operational surprises.
objectives: You build it, you run it
choices: 'You build it, you run it': the building team owns operations (pager, SLOs, runbooks), with SRE/platform enabling via paved roads — align incentives with reality
scenarios.hint: Who feels the 3am page from a design shortcut?
scenarios.why: The split misaligns incentives: builders don't feel operational pain, so they don't design for it. Ownership reunification (builders run it, enabled by platforms) makes operability a design input. Choices 2/3/4 optimize the handoff instead of removing it. Correct: unify build and run ownership.

scenarios.title: Stale runbook extends incident
scenarios.situation: An incident ran 40 minutes longer because the runbook's commands referenced a retired tool. Last tested: never.
choices: Quarterly runbook testing (execute or dry-run every command), linked from alerts, with drift treated as a bug — plus coverage metrics
scenarios.hint: When was the last time anyone ran those commands?
scenarios.why: Untested runbooks are incident-extenders: the responder discovers the drift mid-crisis. Quarterly execution (or dry-run), alert linkage, and coverage metrics keep them honest. Choice 2/3 reduce coverage. Choice 4 is the tribal-knowledge trap. Correct: test like code.

scenarios.title: Prioritizing reliability work
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks 'where should SRE focus?' Five teams lobby with anecdotes; the loudest wins every quarter.
choices: Operational maturity assessments: score every service on SLOs, alerting, runbooks, toil, DR (1-5 each) — lowest scores on most-critical services get SRE engagement first
scenarios.hint: What would prove which team needs SRE most?
scenarios.why: Anecdotes allocate by volume; maturity scores allocate by need. The rubric (scored axes × service criticality) produces a defensible priority list and a re-measurable baseline. Choices 2/3/4 are all politics by other means. Correct: assess, score, prioritize.

scenarios.title: The immortal 'temporary' service
scenarios.situation: A 'temporary' migration service from 2021 still runs, unowned, unpatched, with production credentials. Nobody dares turn it off.
choices: Decommissioning as a project: owner assigned, consumers notified, migration plan, shutdown date enforced, credentials rotated — 'temporary' needs an expiry date at creation
scenarios.hint: What was the expiry date on 'temporary'?
scenarios.why: Temporary without an expiry becomes permanent and unowned — a security and toil liability. Decommissioning is project work: owner, notices, plan, enforced date. Choice 2 accepts the risk. Choice 3 is reckless. Choice 4 observes without acting. And going forward: every 'temporary' service gets a shutdown date at birth. Correct: project-managed shutdown.

scenarios.title: Invisible ownership
scenarios.situation: During an incident, 20 minutes were spent figuring out who owns the failing service. Three teams pointed at each other.
choices: A service catalog: every service with exactly one owner, SLOs, runbooks, on-call rotation — the incident's first lookup, kept current
scenarios.hint: What should the IC look up in the first 60 seconds?
scenarios.why: 20 minutes of owner-hunting during an incident is pure waste — and it recurs every incident. The catalog makes ownership a lookup, not an investigation. A wiki (choice 3) rots; the catalog is structured and reviewed. Choices 2/4 don't address the lookup. Correct: living service catalog.

domains.summary: Service ownership: who owns reliability and how ownership is exercised.

domains.name: Reliability Leadership & Advocacy
domains.description: Negotiating SLOs with product, reliability roadmaps, and leading cultural change.

scenarios.title: Product vs SRE on nines
scenarios.situation: Product insists on 99.99% for a new feature; SRE's math shows 99.9% suffices for users and 99.99% doubles cost and halves velocity. Stalemate.
scenarios.prompt: How does the SRE lead resolve it?
choices: Bring the business case: user-impact data, cost per nine, velocity cost — then document the agreed SLO with review date. Negotiate with numbers, not philosophy
scenarios.hint: What would change product's mind — argument or arithmetic?
scenarios.why: Stalemates break on data: what do users actually feel at 99.9% vs 99.99%? What does the extra nine cost in dollars and shipped features? The lead's job is translating reliability into business terms and documenting the decision. Choices 2/3 abdicate one side. Choice 4 escalates what data can resolve. Correct: negotiate with numbers.

scenarios.title: Roadmap without sequencing
scenarios.situation: The reliability roadmap lists 20 initiatives with no order, no owners, no metrics. A year later, 3 are done.
choices: Sequence by leverage (SLOs → alerting → toil → advanced), one owner and one metric per item, quarterly review with leadership — a roadmap is a commitment device
scenarios.hint: What distinguishes item #1 from item #20?
scenarios.why: Unordered, unowned, unmeasured lists aren't roadmaps — they're wishes. Sequencing by leverage (foundations first), ownership, metrics, and quarterly review turn the list into execution. Choice 2 helps but doesn't fix structure. Correct: sequenced, owned, measured, reviewed.

scenarios.title: Ticket-count reporting
scenarios.situation: The monthly reliability report lists tickets closed and deploys run. Leadership can't tell if reliability is improving.
evidence: 'are we more reliable than last quarter?' — unanswerable
choices: Business-language reliability: SLO compliance trends, budget health, incident/MTTR trends, toil trajectory, and 1-2 specific asks — one page, trends not snapshots
No report; reliability speaks for itself
scenarios.hint: What would tell leadership reliability improved?
scenarios.why: Tickets and deploys measure activity, not reliability. Leadership needs: are we meeting SLOs (trend), is the budget healthy, are incidents falling, is toil shrinking — plus what you need from them. One page, monthly, honest about misses. Correct: outcome metrics + asks.

scenarios.title: Mandate-first culture change
scenarios.situation: Leadership mandates 'blameless postmortems' by decree. Teams comply on paper; behavior unchanged; postmortems still thin.
choices: Systems over slogans: pilot with willing teams, publish wins, embed practices in templates and policies (the easy path becomes the blameless path), measure adoption — mandates don't create safety
scenarios.hint: What makes blamelessness the easy path, not the mandated one?
scenarios.why: Culture follows systems: when the postmortem template, facilitator training, and leadership modeling make blamelessness the easy path, behavior follows. Decrees (choices 2/4) breed compliance theater. Training alone (choice 3) without system change fades. Correct: pilot, prove, systematize, measure.

scenarios.title: 'What's the ROI of SRE?'
scenarios.situation: The CFO asks for SRE's ROI before approving headcount. The team has only anecdotes: 'we prevented outages'.
choices: Quantify: incident cost avoided (downtime $/min × MTTR reduction), toil hours reclaimed (× loaded cost), velocity gained (deploy frequency × feature value) — with the measurement systems to keep proving it
scenarios.hint: What does an hour of checkout downtime cost?
scenarios.why: 'Priceless' (choice 2) loses budget fights; threats (choice 3) lose trust. The professional answer quantifies: MTTR reduction × cost-per-minute, toil reclaimed, velocity unlocked — and builds the metrics to keep proving it quarterly. Correct: ROI in the CFO's language.

scenarios.title: Losing automators
scenarios.situation: The best SRE automators keep leaving for product teams: 'more scope, better ladder'. The SRE org is left with ticket-handlers.
choices: Real scope and ladder in SRE: Staff+ roles defined by reliability leverage (practices adopted org-wide, toil eliminated at scale), high-impact automation charters — make SRE the place ambitious engineers grow
scenarios.hint: Where can an ambitious automator have the most leverage here?
scenarios.why: Talent follows growth and impact: if SRE offers neither beyond Senior, automators leave. The fix is structural — Staff+ scope in reliability terms, charter-level automation work, visible org-wide impact. Counter-offers (choice 2) are one-time. Choice 3 is coercive. Correct: make SRE a destination, not a waystation.

scenarios.title: Hiding the miss
scenarios.situation: The monthly report shows all SLOs green — but the team knows the checkout SLO was breached for 6 hours (excluded as 'anomaly').
choices: Report the breach plainly with cause and fix: credibility is the currency that buys future reliability investment — sugarcoating destroys it exactly when needed
Keep it green; it was anomalous
Redefine the SLO to exclude anomalies
scenarios.hint: What happens to the next budget ask if leadership discovers the exclusion?
scenarios.why: Excluding the breach corrupts the metric and — worse — teaches leadership the numbers can't be trusted. Honest reporting (breach + cause + fix) builds the credibility that funds the next ask. Choices 2/3/4 all trade short-term comfort for long-term trust. Correct: plain honesty, with the fix.
