lessons.title: SRE Practices — Core concepts
concepts: SLIs measure what users experience: success rate, latency percentiles, freshness. SLOs set the target (e.g., 99.9% of requests succeed). Resource metrics inform capacity; they are not SLIs.

The error budget is the allowed unreliability (100% − SLO) over a window. Budget remaining → ship fast; budget exhausted → reliability work takes priority. The trade-off is negotiated in advance, not during incidents.
Burn-rate alerting ties pages to the budget: fast-burn (e.g., 14.4× over 1h/5m windows) pages a human; slow-burn (6× over 6h/30m) files a ticket. Multi-window pairs reset promptly when burning stops.

Incident response is a coordination discipline first: declare, assign roles (commander, comms, ops), run a rhythm, communicate outward. Blameless postmortems fix systems, not people — human error is the starting point, never the root cause.
Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable work with no enduring value. Cap it, then automate it away — hiring into toil just scales the toil.

example.code:
rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[1h]) / rate(http_requests_total[1h])
# fast-burn alert: 14.4x budget burn over 1h long / 5m short windows
# slow-burn alert: 6x budget burn over 6h long / 30m short windows
example.walkthrough: The error-ratio expression underlying burn-rate alerts: divide the 5xx rate by the total rate. Compare against the burn-rate thresholds derived from your SLO — fast burn pages, slow burn tickets.

pitfalls: Common trap: SLIs on CPU/memory — green dashboards while users see errors.
Common trap: single-threshold alerts — they page on spikes and miss slow bleeds; use multi-window burn rates.
Common trap: 'be more careful' as a postmortem action item — it fixes nothing; fix the system that allowed the mistake.
Common trap: hiring to absorb toil instead of automating it — toil scales with growth, automation compounds.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Sre Practices move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of SRE Practices
concepts: SRE Practices is a multi-step process within SRE Practices: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect SRE Practices to the broader SRE Practices ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  SRE Practices begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to SRE Practices. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating SRE Practices as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the full SRE Practices flow from memory. Label every handoff and dependency.

lessons.title: Welcome: how this CBT is built
concepts: This bootcamp teaches SRE as a practice and culture: error budgets, blamelessness, postmortems, toil elimination, org models, sustainable on-call, launch readiness, DR, ownership, and reliability leadership.
Each domain has lessons (concepts + worked examples), scenario drills (realistic situations testing judgment), and hands-on labs (doing the practice yourself).
The mock-assessment domain assembles scenarios from every domain into a timed run — save it for the end of each study cycle.
SRE practices are about how teams behave under pressure and how they learn: the through-line is turning incidents and toil into systematic improvement.

example.code:
The SRE practices loop:
1. Error budget sets the reliability target
2. Incidents spend the budget → blameless postmortem
3. Action items eliminate toil and harden the system
4. Launch reviews protect the budget going forward
5. Culture sustains the loop
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: every domain in this bootcamp owns one step of the loop. Practices reinforce each other — blameless culture makes postmortems honest, which makes toil elimination accurate.

pitfalls: Treating SRE as a tool list instead of practices
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Study strategy: spaced, mixed, and applied
concepts: Spaced repetition beats cramming: revisit each domain 1 day, 3 days, and 7 days after first contact. The domain order is your review schedule.
Interleave domains: after postmortems, do blameless-culture scenarios before moving on. Mixing forces discrimination — exactly what interviews test.
Practices must be performed, not just read: write a real postmortem, run a real toil audit, draft a real launch checklist. The labs make you do this.
Track your misses: when a scenario's 'why' surprises you, re-do that domain's lab before moving on.

example.code:
Study loop:
Day 1: Lessons + scenarios for one domain
Day 2: Labs for that domain + 5 scenarios from the previous domain
Day 7: Mock assessment mixing all domains so far
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the loop alternates learning (lessons), judgment (scenarios), and doing (labs), with built-in spaced review. Practices compound — the capstone assumes all of them.

pitfalls: Reading about postmortems without writing one
Doing scenarios once and never revisiting misses
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: What SRE interviews actually test
concepts: Methodology interviews test judgment and stories: 'tell me about a postmortem that changed something' — they want the arc, the conflict, and the outcome.
The five classic deep-dives: facilitating a blameless postmortem, eliminating a toil source, negotiating an SLO with product, designing an on-call rotation, running a launch review.
Prepare two stories per domain: one success (practice worked) and one lesson (practice was missing). Interviewers probe the lesson stories hardest.
Culture questions are not softballs: 'how do you handle blame in reviews?' has right and wrong answers. The blameless-culture domain is interview armor.

example.code:
Story shape (problem → practice → outcome):
'Alerts paged 12x/night (problem) → ran a toil audit, automated top 3, set alert-quality SLO (practice) → 1 page/week, on-call NPS up (outcome)'
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the shape works for every domain — name the problem, the practice you applied, and the measured outcome. Rehearse until each story fits in 2 minutes.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: The core mental models
concepts: Error budgets govern: reliability is a budget to spend deliberately, not a maximum to achieve. Every practice serves the budget.
Blamelessness enables learning: people hide information when they fear punishment; hidden information kills postmortems. Safety first, always.
Toil is the enemy: manual repetitive work scales linearly with the system while the team doesn't — automate or drown.
SRE is engineering applied to operations: software practices (testing, code review, automation) applied to running systems.

example.code:
Four models, one sentence each:
Budgets: spend reliability deliberately.
Blameless: safety produces truth.
Toil: automate the repetitive.
Engineering: operations as software.
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: when a scenario confuses you, return to these — the right answer almost always serves one of the four. They are the tiebreakers for ambiguous situations.

pitfalls: Optimizing one model while violating another
Treating models as slogans, not decision tools
Forgetting the budget when it matters most
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets: the foundation
concepts: SLIs measure user-facing reliability (success rate, latency percentiles); SLOs set the target; the error budget (1 - SLO) is the allowed unreliability — the governance mechanism.
Choose SLIs from the user's perspective: what the user experiences, not what the server reports. 2-4 SLIs per service is plenty.
The budget converts debates into arithmetic: budget healthy → ship; budget exhausted → freeze features and pay down reliability debt.
Write the budget policy down: thresholds, who decides, what 'exhausted' triggers. An undocumented budget is a suggestion.

example.code:
SLO: 99.9% success over 30d → 43.2 min budget.
Policy: <50% remaining → normal; exhausted → feature freeze.
Owner: service team; arbiter: SRE.
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the policy is what makes the SLO real. Without the freeze clause and named owners, the budget is a dashboard decoration nobody acts on.

pitfalls: SLIs on server metrics users never see
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Incident response discipline
concepts: Incidents follow a discipline: declare roles (commander, comms, ops), mitigate before diagnosing, communicate on cadence, and record a timeline.
Mitigation first: roll back, kill the flag, shift traffic — understanding can wait until users are safe. Pre-authorize the IC to mitigate without tickets.
Comms discipline: updates every 15-30 min, impact first, separate channels for responders/customers/execs. Silence breeds panic and interruptions.
Every incident produces a timeline; every significant incident produces a postmortem. No timeline, no learning.

example.code:
First 5 minutes:
1. Declare: 'I'm IC, Ana has comms, Ben on ops'
2. Impact: 'checkout 5xx 8%, started 14:15'
3. Mitigate: 'rolling back 1.4.2 now'
4. Timeline started; next update 14:30
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: five minutes of structure prevents an hour of chaos. The IC coordinates; comms shields the responders; ops executes the pre-written mitigations.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Eliminating toil systematically
concepts: Toil: manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, no enduring value. It's the work that scales with the system while headcount doesn't.
Measure it: toil hours per on-call shift, manual deploy counts, ticket volumes. Cap it: keep operational work under 50% of SRE time, toil trending to zero.
Eliminate in order: document the runbook, script it, schedule it, then delete the manual path. Deleting the manual path is the actual win.
Prioritize by frequency × pain × error rate. The weekly 2-hour painful task beats the yearly 10-minute one.

example.code:
Toil audit → backlog:
- manual deploys 34/mo → automate top 3 flows
- cert renewals by hand → ACME
- toil 6h/shift → target < 2h
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the audit turns complaints into a prioritized backlog with numbers. Each item gets the document→script→schedule→delete treatment.

pitfalls: Keeping the manual path 'just in case'
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Monitoring and alerting philosophy
concepts: Monitor from the user's perspective: the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) per service, symptoms over causes.
Alert on burn rate, not raw counts: pages for 'needs human action now', tickets for the rest. Every alert needs a runbook, severity, and owner.
Alert fatigue is a reliability bug: measure pages per shift and actionability; tune or delete noisy alerts like any other defect.
Dashboards serve incidents: SLI-first layout, deploy annotations, variables not hardcoding. Review quarterly; delete the unused.

example.code:
alert: CheckoutBurn
condition: 'burn rate 14x over 1h'
action: page
runbook: 'https://runbooks/checkout-burn'
# NOT: 'CPU > 90%' with no runbook
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the symptom-based alert with a runbook is actionable at 3am; the CPU alert is a puzzle. Philosophy made concrete: alert on what users feel, with the fix one click away.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Capacity planning as a practice
concepts: Capacity planning is a recurring practice, not a spreadsheet: measure cost-per-request under load, provision for peak × headroom, revisit quarterly.
Headroom covers variance and failure: N+1 for zone loss plus growth buffer. Write assumptions down — they're the first thing to revisit.
Load test to breaking quarterly: find the real bottleneck and record the breaking point. Unknown limits are just hope.
Plan the dependencies too: your service scales, but does the connection pool? The downstream quota? Plans die at unmodeled dependencies.

example.code:
Capacity review (quarterly):
peak RPS, cost/request, headroom %, breaking point,
dependency limits, growth forecast → provisioned capacity
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the review is the practice — same inputs, refreshed numbers, explicit assumptions. A plan with an expiry date beats a perfect one-time spreadsheet.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: The SRE engagement model
concepts: SRE teams engage with product teams through defined interfaces: SLO reviews, launch readiness, incident collaboration — not ticket queues.
The error budget mediates the relationship: healthy budget → SRE helps ship faster; exhausted → SRE work shifts to reliability until recovered.
SREs embed temporarily to bootstrap practices, then leave: the goal is product teams owning their reliability, not permanent SRE ownership.
Measure the engagement: % of services with SLOs, postmortem action completion, toil trends. The engagement either improves these or it's theater.

example.code:
Engagement lifecycle:
1. Assess: SLOs? runbooks? toil level?
2. Bootstrap: SLO workshop, alert overhaul (6-8 weeks)
3. Hand back: team owns; SRE advises
4. Measure: SLO coverage, toil trend
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: time-boxed, outcome-measured, ending in handoff — the opposite of permanent ticket-queue ownership. The metrics prove whether the engagement worked.

pitfalls: SRE as a permanent ticket queue
Engagements with no end date or metrics
SRE owning services instead of enabling teams
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Budget math: windows and calculations
concepts: Error budget = (1 - SLO) × window: 99.9% over 30 days = 0.1% × 43,200 min = 43.2 minutes of allowed badness.
Window choice matters: 30-day rolling smooths noise and matches business cadence; 7-day reacts faster but punishes one bad day disproportionately.
Track budget as remaining %, not just consumed minutes: '62% remaining with 9 days left' is the decision-ready form.
Composite services need budget allocation: if checkout depends on 3 services at 99.9%, checkout can't promise 99.9% — budgets compose multiplicatively.

example.code:
Budget math:
99.9% / 30d → 43.2 min
99.95% / 30d → 21.6 min
99.99% / 30d → 4.3 min
Remaining: (1 - bad_minutes/43.2) × 100
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the 99.99% line shows why the last nines are expensive — 4.3 minutes per month leaves no room for deploys, experiments, or bad luck. Choose SLOs with the arithmetic in view.

pitfalls: Quoting SLOs without computing the budget
Window too short for the business cadence
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Burn rates: fast vs slow
concepts: Burn rate = how fast you're consuming budget relative to even pace: 1x = exactly on track; 14x = gone in ~2 days.
Fast-burn alerts (1h window): catch cliffs — page. Slow-burn alerts (6h-3d): catch leaks — ticket. Both reference the same budget.
Set thresholds from the budget, not from gut: page when burning 2% of monthly budget per hour; ticket at 10x the sustainable rate over 6h.
Burn-rate alerting self-adjusts to traffic: quiet at 3am, proportional at peak. It ends the '5 errors paged me' era.

example.code:
# fast burn: 14.4x budget consumption, 1h window
sum(rate(errors[1h]))/sum(rate(requests[1h])) > 0.001*14.4
# slow burn: 6x, 6h window → ticket
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: thresholds as multiples of the budgeted error rate adapt to traffic automatically. The two windows catch different failure shapes — cliffs vs leaks.

pitfalls: Thresholds from gut, not budget math
Alerting on raw counts instead of rates
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Budget policy: what happens at zero
concepts: The policy is the point: define exactly what changes at 50%, 100%, and negative (overdrawn) budget — feature freeze, launch reviews, paging changes.
Freezes must be scoped: freeze risky launches, not all work — reliability work and small safe fixes continue. Overbroad freezes get violated.
Someone must own the decision: name the arbiter (SRE lead, service owner) empowered to call the freeze. Committees don't work at 2am.
Recovery criteria: the freeze lifts when the budget recovers to X% — defined in advance, not negotiated mid-incident.

example.code:
Budget policy:
≤50% remaining: normal velocity
<50%: launches need SRE review
0% (exhausted): freeze risky launches
Recovery: freeze lifts at 25% remaining
Arbiter: on-call SRE lead
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: every line removes a future argument. The team knows the rules before the budget runs out — that's what makes the freeze legitimate instead of political.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Budgets and launch decisions
concepts: Launches spend budget: every release risks errors. Gate risky launches on budget health — full budget → proceed; thin budget → extra validation or delay.
New services start with no budget history: give them a provisional SLO and review after 30 days of data. Don't launch blind, don't block on perfection.
Big launches get budget reservations: earmark X% of the budget for the launch window, with rollback criteria defined before launch.
Post-launch budget review: did the launch consume what we predicted? The gap calibrates future launch risk assessments.

example.code:
Launch gate:
budget > 50% → launch with standard canary
budget 20-50% → launch with 2x canary duration + SRE review
budget < 20% → delay unless exec-approved
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the gate is proportional — it doesn't block launches, it scales their caution to the remaining budget. Teams learn to check the budget before scheduling launches.

pitfalls: Same launch process regardless of budget
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Multi-service budgets and composition
concepts: User-facing SLOs compose from dependencies: checkout at 99.9% needs its dependencies strictly better — 3 deps at 99.9% ≈ 99.7% composed.
Allocate budgets top-down: the product SLO determines each dependency's required SLO. Dependencies that can't meet it need redundancy or fallbacks.
Shared platforms need budget contracts with consumers: 'the platform offers 99.95%; your service's SLO must account for the 0.05%'.
Review composition quarterly: new dependencies silently erode the composed SLO. The dependency map is a living document.

example.code:
Composition:
checkout SLO 99.9% needs:
  payments ≥99.95%, inventory ≥99.95%, auth ≥99.99%
Composed: 0.9995×0.9995×0.9999 ≈ 99.89% — shortfall!
→ add fallback or tighten a dep
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the multiplication exposes the shortfall before users do. The fix is structural (fallback, redundancy) not aspirational ('try harder').

pitfalls: Assuming dependency SLOs equal your SLO
No budget contracts with platform teams
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: What blameless actually means
concepts: Blameless doesn't mean no accountability — it means separating the person from the system: ask 'what allowed this?' not 'who did this?'
Accountability in blameless culture = owning the fix and the learning, not absorbing punishment. 'I shipped the bug; here's the guardrail I added' is the model.
Blame looks like: naming people in incident titles, performance consequences for outages, 'be more careful' as an action item. All three kill honesty.
The test: would an engineer volunteer 'I caused this' in the postmortem? If not, you're not blameless yet — regardless of what the values slide says.

example.code:
Blameless language:
✗ 'Ana deployed the bad config'
✓ 'The deploy pipeline allowed an unvalidated config'
✗ Action: 'Ana will be more careful'
✓ Action: 'Add config schema validation to CI'
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the rewrite moves the cause from the person to the system and the action from vigilance to engineering. That's the entire practice in one example.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Psychological safety: the prerequisite
concepts: Psychological safety = people can report bad news, admit mistakes, and disagree without fear. It's the soil blamelessness grows in.
Leaders create it by modeling: admitting their own mistakes publicly, thanking people who surface problems, never punishing messengers.
Measure it: anonymous surveys ('I can report a mistake without fear'), and behavioral signals (do juniors speak in reviews? do people volunteer bad news?).
Safety is built in small moments: how the first question after an incident is phrased, whether the intern's concern gets heard, what happens to the whistleblower.

example.code:
Safety signals (monthly pulse):
- 'I can admit a mistake here' (1-5)
- 'Bad news travels up quickly' (1-5)
- behavioral: junior speak-up rate in reviews
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the survey makes safety discussable; the behavioral signals verify it. Leaders review these like any other health metric — because they are.

pitfalls: Assuming safety from a values statement

lessons.title: Running blameless reviews
concepts: Facilitation matters more than templates: the facilitator protects safety — redirects blame language, draws out quiet voices, keeps focus on systems.
Ground rules stated upfront: no blame, no rank in the room, curiosity over judgment, every perspective valid. Repeat them every time until they're culture.
Structure: timeline walkthrough (what happened), then 'five whys' on system causes, then action items. The timeline prevents narrative wars.
Handle blame in real time: 'let's rephrase — what in the system allowed that action?' Said kindly, firmly, every time.

example.code:
Facilitator script:
'Ground rules: no blame, no rank, curiosity first.'
'Timeline first — what did we observe, minute by minute?'
(On blame): 'What allowed that? What would stop it next time?'
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the script is short because the skill is in the moment — redirecting blame kindly but immediately, before it chills the room. Facilitation is a trained skill; rotate and coach facilitators.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Blamelessness under pressure: execs and customers
concepts: Pressure flows downhill: execs demanding 'who caused this?' will get blame unless SRE leadership translates — 'here's the systemic cause and the fix'.
Prepare the narrative before the exec review: timeline, system causes, action items with owners and dates. Execs accept blameless when they see rigor.
Customer comms stay blameless too: 'a configuration change caused...' not 'an engineer mistakenly...'. Customers want the fix, not a scapegoat.
If leadership punishes despite the practice, say so plainly in the retro: 'the policy says blameless; the consequence said otherwise' — culture is what happens, not what's written.

example.code:
Exec summary template:
Impact → timeline → systemic causes (3) →
fixes shipped (2) → in flight (3, owners+dates) →
'no individual fault; process gaps addressed'
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the template gives execs what they need (impact, fixes, dates) in blameless language. Rigor is what earns leadership's trust in the practice.

pitfalls: Throwing someone under the bus for execs
Ignoring the gap between policy and consequences
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Just culture: the boundary of blameless
concepts: Blameless has a boundary: just culture distinguishes honest mistakes (system fix), at-risk behavior (coaching), and reckless violations (consequences).
Honest mistake: followed process, system allowed the error → fix the system. At-risk: shortcutted process under pressure → coach, fix the pressure. Reckless: knowing violation → consequences.
The categories must be defined in advance and applied consistently — retroactive categorization feels like blame regardless of intent.
Most incidents are honest mistakes or at-risk behavior. If everything looks reckless, the system (or the definition) is wrong.

example.code:
Just-culture triage:
- honest mistake → system fix, no individual action
- at-risk behavior → coaching + fix the incentive/pressure
- reckless → defined consequences (rare; defined in policy)
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the triage protects blamelessness from its failure mode ('no accountability for anything') while keeping consequences rare, defined, and fair. Write the definitions before you need them.

pitfalls: No written definitions of the categories

lessons.title: Anatomy of an effective postmortem
concepts: Structure: summary, impact (users, duration, magnitude), timeline, root causes (plural — there's never one), what went well, what didn't, action items.
Impact first: the reader should know the user cost in the first paragraph. 'Checkout 5xx at 8% for 42 min, ~$180k at risk' beats three paragraphs of architecture.
Root causes are systemic: 'deploy pipeline lacked config validation' not 'Ana'. List contributing factors — the outage needed all of them.
Length proportional to impact: SEV1 gets the full treatment; SEV3 gets a paragraph. Template, don't bureaucratize.

example.code:
Postmortem skeleton:
# Summary (3 lines)  # Impact (users, $, duration)
# Timeline  # Root causes (systemic, plural)
# Went well / poorly  # Action items (owner+date each)
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the skeleton fits on one page for most incidents. Impact-first respects the reader; plural root causes respect reality; owner+date on every action respects follow-through.

pitfalls: Action items without owners or dates
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Timelines: the factual backbone
concepts: Build the timeline from logs, chat, and tool timestamps — not memory. Memory compresses, reorders, and self-serves.
Include: detection time, each mitigation attempt, comms sent, decisions made and by whom. The gaps ('nothing happened 14:20-14:45') are data too.
Distinguish observed vs inferred: '14:22 errors dropped (observed)' vs 'rollback likely caused it (inferred)'. Conflation corrupts learning.
The timeline often reveals the real story: the fix that worked by accident, the 25-minute gap nobody noticed, the alert that fired but was missed.

example.code:
Timeline excerpt:
14:15 errors begin (observed, dashboard)
14:18 IC declared (chat)
14:20 rollback started (deploy log)
14:20-14:45 no comms sent (gap!)
14:45 errors falling (observed)
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the 25-minute comms gap is the kind of finding only a timestamped timeline surfaces — and it becomes an action item ('comms template + timer').

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Action items that actually get done
concepts: Every action item: single owner, due date, and a definition of done. 'Improve monitoring' is not an action item; 'Add burn-rate alert with runbook by Fri' is.
Prioritize: P0 (prevent recurrence), P1 (detect faster), P2 (nice hardening). P0s get sprint capacity reserved — typically 10-20% for postmortem work.
Track to completion publicly: a postmortem-action dashboard, reviewed weekly. Items older than 30 days get escalated, not forgotten.
Close the loop: when an action ships, link it back to the postmortem. The team sees that postmortems cause change — that's what makes the next one honest.

example.code:
Action item format:
[P0] Add config schema validation to CI — owner: Ben, due: Fri
Done =: invalid config fails the build (demo in review)
Tracked: postmortem-actions board, reviewed Mondays
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: owner + date + done-definition makes the item real; the board makes it visible; the demo closes the loop. Vague items die quietly — specific ones ship.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Postmortem facilitation skills
concepts: The facilitator is neutral: not the incident's protagonist, not the team's manager. Neutrality lets them protect safety and ask dumb questions.
Draw out quiet voices: 'Priya, you were watching the DB — what did you see?' The best insights often come from observers, not actors.
Manage the narrative wars: when two people disagree on what happened, go to the timeline. Data settles stories.
End with the learning: 'what's the one thing we'll do differently?' If the room can't name it, the postmortem isn't done.

example.code:
Facilitator moves:
- open: ground rules + timeline
- probe: 'what surprised you?'
- redirect: blame → system question
- close: 'one thing we'll change?' + owners/dates
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: 'what surprised you?' is the highest-yield question — surprises mark the gap between mental model and reality, which is exactly what postmortems exist to close.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Postmortem culture: cadence and readership
concepts: Hold postmortems for every SEV1/SEV2 and for interesting SEV3s — within days, while memory is fresh and logs are hot.
Publish widely: the whole org can read postmortems (sanitized). Other teams learn from your incidents — that's the multiplier.
Review postmortem quality quarterly: are action items completing? Are the same causes recurring? Recurring causes mean the actions aren't working.
Celebrate good postmortems: the honest, insightful ones get highlighted. What gets celebrated gets repeated.

example.code:
Postmortem health metrics:
- held within 5 days: 95%
- action completion in 30d: 80%
- repeat-cause incidents: trending down
- readership: 60% of engineers read last quarter's
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the metrics measure the practice, not the incidents. Repeat causes trending down is the ultimate proof the loop works.

pitfalls: No quality metrics on the practice

lessons.title: Toil taxonomy: recognizing it
concepts: Toil's markers: manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical (not strategic), no enduring value, scales with service growth.
Common species: manual deploys, ticket-driven provisioning, hand-run data fixes, manual cert renewals, copy-paste config changes, toil disguised as 'ops work'.
Not toil: novel incident response, one-off migrations, design work, anything done once. Repetition is what converts work into toil.
The toil test: 'if the service 10x'd, would this task 10x?' If yes and it's manual, it's toil — and it's a scaling risk, not just an annoyance.

example.code:
Toil or not?
- manual deploy #34 this month → toil
- first-ever region failover → engineering
- hand-editing firewall rules weekly → toil
- designing the new alerting scheme → engineering
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the 10x test separates scaling risks from one-off efforts. Naming the species (manual deploys, ticket provisioning) makes the audit concrete.

pitfalls: No shared definition on the team
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Measuring toil: the audit
concepts: Run a quarterly toil audit: sample on-call weeks, classify every task, total the toil hours. Data beats anecdotes in prioritization fights.
Track: toil hours per shift, % of ops time that's toil, top toil sources by frequency × duration, toil trend over quarters.
Source the data from tickets, deploy logs, and chat — not just memory. Memory undercounts the small repetitive tasks that dominate.
Publish the results: the audit is a forcing function. 'We spent 38% of on-call on toil last quarter' starts the right conversations.

example.code:
Audit output:
Q3: 38% of on-call hours = toil (target <15%)
Top sources: manual deploys (34), cert renewals (6), quota tickets (98)
→ Q4 automation backlog, top 3 funded
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the percentage makes toil discussable at the leadership level; the ranked list makes it actionable at the team level. Both are needed.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: The automation playbook
concepts: Order: document the manual process → script it → add dry-run → schedule/trigger it → monitor it → delete the manual path.
Automations need production discipline: idempotent, logged, monitored, with rollback and a manual escape hatch. A flaky script is worse than toil.
ROI ordering: frequency × pain × error-rate. Automate the weekly painful error-prone task before the monthly trivial one.
Deleting the manual path is the step that counts: otherwise you maintain two systems and the toil creeps back.

example.code:
# toil automation checklist
# [ ] runbook documented  [ ] idempotent script
# [ ] dry-run mode  [ ] monitoring + alerts
# [ ] escape hatch  [ ] manual path DELETED
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the checklist is the quality gate. The deleted-manual-path checkbox is last because it's the proof — everything before it is preparation.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Self-service as toil elimination
concepts: The highest-leverage automation removes the ticket: self-service provisioning, one-click rollbacks, self-serve quota increases within guardrails.
Guardrails not gates: quotas, templates, policy checks replace human approvers. The user succeeds alone; the system stays safe.
Measure deflection: % of requests completed without a ticket. The ticket queue shrinking is the KPI.
Start with the top 3 ticket types — they usually cover 70%+ of volume. Exotic requests can wait.

example.code:
Ticket analysis:
1. 'provision dev env' 212/q → self-service button
2. 'quota increase' 98/q → auto-approve < limit
3. 'secret rotation' 61/q → one-click
Deflection target: 80% within 2 quarters
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the ticket data tells you exactly what to build. Three automations, 371 tickets/quarter eliminated — the queue visibly shrinks and the team reclaims the hours.

lessons.title: Sustaining: keeping toil down
concepts: Toil regrows: every new manual process is future toil. Gate new operational processes on 'how will this be automated?'
Toil budget: cap the % of sprint capacity spent on toil-driven work; new toil sources get automation backlog items, not shrugs.
On-call handoff includes toil notes: 'this alert paged 4x, needs tuning' — the next shift continues the elimination.
Celebrate eliminations: 'we deleted the deploy runbook' is a win worth announcing. Culture sustains what process starts.

example.code:
Sustaining mechanisms:
- new processes: automation plan required
- sprint: 15% capacity reserved for toil automation
- on-call handoff: toil notes section
- wins announced in team demo
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the mechanisms make toil elimination the default, not a campaign. Reserved capacity is the keystone — without it, automation loses to feature work every sprint.

pitfalls: One-time toil project, no sustaining mechanisms

lessons.title: SRE vs DevOps vs Platform Engineering
concepts: DevOps is a philosophy (collaboration, automation, shared ownership); SRE is a specific implementation (Google's: SLOs, error budgets, toil caps); Platform Engineering builds the internal platforms both use.
They're complementary, not competing: DevOps culture + SRE practices + platform products = the modern reliability stack.
The confusion costs: teams rebranded 'SRE' doing ticket-queue ops, or 'DevOps teams' that are just ops with pipelines. Names don't create practices.
Hire/organize for the practices you need: if nobody owns SLOs and error budgets, you don't have SRE regardless of titles.

example.code:
Mapping:
DevOps → culture: 'you build it, you run it'
SRE → practice: SLOs, budgets, blameless, toil elimination
Platform → product: paved roads, self-service, golden paths
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the mapping ends the turf war — each has a distinct job. A team can (and should) draw on all three.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: SRE team topologies
concepts: Embedded: SREs in product teams — deep context, but practices diverge and SREs get absorbed into feature work.
Centralized: one SRE team serving many — consistent practices, but becomes a ticket queue without strong engagement models.
Federated/consulting: central SRE sets standards and consults; product teams implement — scales best, needs real authority behind the standards.
Choose by org size and maturity: startups embed; enterprises federate; centralize only with engagement discipline and toil caps.

example.code:
Topology picker:
< 50 engineers: embedded SREs
50-500: federated (central standards + embedded practitioners)
500+: federated + platform teams
Anti-pattern: central ticket-queue 'SRE'
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the picker is a starting point — the engagement model (time-boxed, metric-backed, ending in handoff) matters more than the boxes on the chart.

pitfalls: Embedded SREs absorbed into feature work

lessons.title: The SRE engagement model
concepts: Engagements are time-boxed partnerships: assess → bootstrap practices → hand back ownership. Typically 6-12 weeks, with defined exit criteria.
Entry criteria protect both sides: the team must commit an engineer and sprint capacity; SRE commits to specific outcomes (SLOs defined, alerts overhauled).
Exit criteria prove it worked: SLOs published, runbooks exist, toil measured, team can operate without SRE. No criteria, no exit — engagements rot.
SREs leave: the goal is teams owning their reliability. Permanent SRE ownership of a product team's service is the failure mode.

example.code:
Engagement contract:
IN: team engineer 50%, SLO workshop week 1
DO: SLOs, burn alerts, runbooks, toil audit (8 wks)
OUT: team demos self-sufficiency; SRE advises quarterly
METRICS: SLO coverage, toil %, action completion
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the contract makes expectations explicit on both sides. The exit criteria are the innovation — they prevent the engagement from becoming permanent staffing.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Staffing SRE: skills and ratios
concepts: SREs are software engineers who do operations: hire for coding ability first — the job is automating operations, not staffing a NOC.
Ratios are workload-derived, not fixed: one SRE team per ~8-12 services is a rule of thumb; the real constraint is toil — if toil exceeds 50%, you're understaffed or under-automated.
Grow SRE with the service footprint, not headcount: new services need SLOs, alerts, runbooks — budget SRE time per launch.
Career path matters: SRE needs a real ladder (not 'ops track'), or your best automators leave for product teams.

example.code:
Staffing signals:
- toil > 50% of SRE time → automate or hire
- services without SLOs growing → engage more
- SRE attrition to product teams → fix the ladder
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the signals are leading indicators — they tell you to act before reliability degrades. Staffing by signals beats staffing by ratio.

pitfalls: Hiring ops backgrounds for an automation job
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Anti-patterns: SRE in name only
concepts: Ticket-queue SRE: the 'SRE team' takes ops tickets from product teams. That's ops with a new title — no SLOs, no budgets, no toil elimination.
SRE as gatekeepers: approvals, CABs, deploy police. SRE enables velocity through safety; gatekeeping is the opposite.
SRE without engineering: if the team can't code, it can't automate — it becomes manual ops that happens to use SRE vocabulary.
Diagnose by practices: does the team own SLOs? Enforce budgets? Eliminate toil? Titles are cheap; practices are the test.

example.code:
SRE-or-not checklist:
[ ] SLOs defined and budgeted
[ ] error budget policy enforced
[ ] toil measured and falling
[ ] postmortems blameless with tracked actions
[ ] team writes code weekly
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the checklist is the audit — run it on any team called SRE. Failing items are the transformation backlog, in priority order.

lessons.title: On-call health: the human system
concepts: On-call is a human system with failure modes: fatigue, burnout, attrition. Design it like any critical system — with margins and monitoring.
Compensation must be explicit: pay, time-off in lieu, or both — documented, not 'exposure'. Uncompensated on-call is a trust destroyer.
Follow-the-sun beats heroic nights: distribute across timezones where possible; where not, keep rotations short and recovery real.
Measure human metrics: pages per shift, sleep interruptions, on-call NPS. These are reliability inputs — exhausted responders make worse decisions.

example.code:
On-call health dashboard:
- pages/shift (target < 2)
- sleep interruptions/week (target 0)
- on-call NPS (target > 30)
- time-to-recovery after night pages (target: next-day light duties)
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the dashboard makes human cost visible to leadership. 'Pages per shift' trending up is an early warning — of attrition, not just annoyance.

lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Rotations that don't burn people
concepts: Rotation length: 1 week is the common sweet spot — long enough for context, short enough to recover. 2+ weeks accumulates fatigue.
Team size matters: fewer than 4-5 people means too-frequent rotations. Below that, merge rotations or hire — don't run a 2-person rotation indefinitely.
Handoff discipline: written handoff (known issues, in-flight work, toil notes), overlap hour for questions, and the outgoing person actually disconnects.
Shadow rotations onboard safely: new members shadow for 2-4 weeks, then take supervised shifts. Nobody's first page should be alone at 3am.

example.code:
Rotation design:
- 5+ engineers, 1-week rotations
- handoff doc: known issues, in-flight, toil notes
- shadow 3 weeks before solo
- post-night-page: light duties next day
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: every element protects the human — size prevents frequency fatigue, handoffs prevent context loss, shadowing prevents terror, recovery prevents accumulation.

lessons.title: Alert fatigue: the reliability killer
concepts: Alert fatigue is a safety issue: responders who've been paged 12 times for nothing will miss the 13th, real one. Treat noisy alerts as defects.
The fix pipeline: measure actionability (% of pages needing action), tune thresholds, aggregate flapping, delete the unactionable. Weekly alert review.
Page budgets: cap pages per shift; breaching the budget triggers an alert-quality sprint. The budget makes fatigue discussable.
Distinguish pages from notifications: page = human action needed now; everything else = ticket, email, dashboard. Most 'alerts' aren't pages.

example.code:
Alert quality review (weekly):
- pages/shift, % actionable (target > 90%)
- top 5 noisiest alerts → tune or delete
- any page without a runbook → write one
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the weekly review is the practice — small, regular, relentless. Alert quality compounds like tech debt in reverse.

lessons.title: Escalation policies that work
concepts: Escalation = getting the right help fast: primary → secondary → manager → wider team, with timeouts that match severity (5/15/30 min).
Escalation is not failure: normalize it. 'I escalated early' should be praised, not questioned. Late escalation is how SEV2s become SEV1s.
Keep the chain current: quarterly review of who's on it, whether timeouts still fit, and whether the escalation actually reaches a human.
Document the 'call anyone' rule: for SEV1, anyone can pull anyone. Hierarchy doesn't survive incidents — say so explicitly.

example.code:
escalation:
  SEV1: 'primary 5m → secondary 5m → manager → all-hands'
  SEV2: 'primary 15m → secondary 15m → manager'
  rule: 'anyone can escalate to anyone for SEV1'
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: timeouts encode urgency; the all-hands rule removes permission-seeking. Reviewing quarterly keeps the chain from rotting as teams change.

lessons.title: Burnout prevention and recovery
concepts: Burnout signals: dreading rotations, cynicism about pages, slower incident response, attrition talk. Managers must watch for these, not wait for resignations.
Structural preventions: sustainable page volume, real recovery time, toil reduction (toil is burnout fuel), and career growth that isn't 'more on-call'.
Recovery is real: after brutal weeks, give time and lightness — not just thanks. 'Thanks for the 60-hour incident week, here's your normal sprint' burns people.
Talk about it: normalize discussing on-call load in 1:1s and retros. Silent suffering is the default; explicit conversation is the fix.

example.code:
Burnout checklist (manager, monthly):
- pages/shift trend per person
- time off actually taken post-incidents
- 1:1 question: 'how's on-call feeling?'
- action when signals appear (not after attrition)
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the checklist makes burnout a managed risk, not a personal failing. Acting on signals — redistributing load, funding automation — is what the checklist is for.

lessons.title: Production readiness reviews
concepts: Readiness reviews gate launches on operational criteria: SLOs defined, dashboards built, alerts with runbooks, rollback tested, capacity planned, on-call trained.
The review is collaborative, not adversarial: SRE + owning team walk the checklist together. Findings become launch blockers or accepted risks — explicitly.
Checklists are versioned and minimal: 15-20 items covering the practices in this bootcamp. Bloated checklists get pencil-whipped.
New services get provisional approval with a 30-day review: launch, measure, revisit. Perfection before launch is the enemy of learning.

example.code:
Readiness checklist (excerpt):
[ ] SLOs + budget policy defined
[ ] burn-rate alerts + runbooks
[ ] rollback tested (1 command)
[ ] capacity plan + load test
[ ] on-call trained + escalation set
[ ] launch risks listed + accepted
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: each item maps to a bootcamp domain — the review is the practices made launch-gating. Accepted risks are written, not assumed.

pitfalls: No provisional path for new services

lessons.title: Launch checklists in practice
concepts: The checklist runs in phases: pre-launch (reviews complete, comms ready), launch (canary, monitor, go/no-go), post-launch (hypercare, budget review).
Go/no-go criteria are defined before launch day: error budget thresholds, canary pass criteria, rollback triggers. Deciding mid-launch under pressure goes badly.
Hypercare: the owning team watches closely for 1-2 weeks post-launch with explicit monitoring and a fast rollback path. Launches don't end at deploy.
Retro the launch: what did we predict vs observe? The gap calibrates the next launch's risk assessment.

example.code:
Launch day script:
T-1h: go/no-go check (budget, canary criteria)
T+0: canary 5% → analysis → 25% → 100%
T+2w: hypercare ends; budget review; launch retro
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the script removes launch-day improvisation. Go/no-go before, canary during, hypercare after — each phase has its practice.

lessons.title: Error-budget-aware launches
concepts: Gate launch risk on budget health: full budget → standard process; thin budget → extended canary + SRE review; exhausted → delay or exec exception.
Reserve budget for big launches: earmark a % for the launch window with pre-defined rollback triggers. The reservation makes the risk explicit.
Dark launches and feature flags de-risk: ship code dark, enable for 1%, ramp with kill switch armed. The flag is the launch's safety net.
Post-launch: reconcile predicted vs actual budget spend. Systematic underestimation means the risk model needs work.

example.code:
Launch risk tiers:
standard: budget > 50%, canary 5→25→100
careful: budget 20-50%, 2x canary, SRE review
hold: budget < 20%, delay or exec sign-off
+ kill switch mandatory for careful/hold
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: proportional caution — the process scales with risk instead of blocking everything or nothing. The kill-switch mandate for risky launches is the key safety property.

pitfalls: Same launch process regardless of risk
No budget reservation for big launches

lessons.title: Rollout strategies from the practices view
concepts: Choose rollout strategy by risk: canary (need regression data), blue-green (need instant rollback), rolling (need efficiency), flags (need instant kill).
The practices lens: does the strategy give you detection (canary analysis), mitigation (rollback/kill), and learning (what did we observe)?
Database changes need expand/contract regardless of strategy: no strategy survives a breaking schema change during coexistence.
Document the strategy choice and its assumptions: 'canary 5%/30min assumes 1k rpm for significance' — assumptions get revisited when traffic changes.

example.code:
Strategy decision record:
checkout v2 → canary (need regression data)
config change → flags (need instant kill)
OS patch → rolling (low risk, efficiency)
Each: detection, mitigation, assumptions listed
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the decision record makes strategy a reasoned choice, not a habit. Listing assumptions is what lets the next engineer know when to choose differently.

pitfalls: Breaking schema changes in any rollout

lessons.title: Post-launch reviews
concepts: Review every significant launch within 2 weeks: predicted vs actual (budget spend, incidents, surprises), and what the gap teaches.
Include the quiet launches too — 'nothing happened' is data: it validates the risk model. Only reviewing failures biases the model.
Feed findings back into the readiness checklist: recurring surprise types become new checklist items. The checklist evolves.
Share launch reviews org-wide: the team launching next quarter learns from this quarter's surprises.

example.code:
Launch review template:
- predicted: budget 5%, 0 incidents
- actual: budget 12%, 1 SEV3 (flag misconfig)
- gap: flag testing gap → checklist += 'flag canary test'
- shared: eng-wide launch notes
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the gap analysis is the learning — it found a checklist hole. Sharing it multiplies the value across teams.

lessons.title: DR planning methodology
concepts: DR planning starts with tiers: classify services by RTO/RPO (Tier 0: minutes; Tier 1: hours; Tier 2: days), get the numbers signed off by stakeholders.
For each tier: the playbook (failover steps), the verification (how you know it worked), and the drill cadence (quarterly for Tier 0).
Dependencies are the plan's weak points: your DR is only as good as your least-drilled dependency. Map and drill them.
The plan lives where the responders are: runbooks, not binders. If the plan isn't executable during an incident, it's fiction.

example.code:
DR plan structure per tier:
- RTO/RPO (signed off)
- failover playbook (tested commands)
- verification checklist
- drill cadence + last drill date
- dependencies + their DR status
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the structure forces completeness — numbers, playbook, proof, schedule, dependencies. Missing any one is a plan with a hole.

lessons.title: Backup and restore testing
concepts: Backups are worthless; restores are everything. Test restores regularly — the industry's most repeated lesson because it's the most ignored.
Test the full restore: from backup media to serving traffic, timed. 'Backup succeeded' is not 'we can recover'.
Include the awkward parts: credentials, DNS, certs, config — restores fail on the un-backed-up secret, not the database.
Automate restore tests: scheduled game-day restores with success criteria. Manual restore tests get skipped; automated ones just run.

2. restore from latest backup (timed)
3. run smoke tests (serving traffic?)
4. report: RTO achieved vs target
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the test proves the RTO instead of asserting it. Timing it monthly catches backup rot before the disaster does.

lessons.title: RTO/RPO from the SRE view
concepts: RTO/RPO are SLOs for disaster: define them per tier, measure drills against them, and treat misses like SLO breaches — with action items.
Derive architecture from the numbers: RPO 1 min rules out async replication with 5-min lag; RTO 15 min rules out manual runbooks.
Cost the tiers: Tier 0 DR is expensive; that's why tiers exist. Present 'RTO 15 min costs $X, RTO 4h costs $Y' and let the business choose.
Review when things change: new dependencies, architecture shifts, business changes. Stale RTO/RPOs design the wrong system.

example.code:
RTO/RPO as SLOs:
Tier 0: RTO 15m, RPO 1m — drilled quarterly, misses → P0 actions
Tier 1: RTO 4h, RPO 1h — drilled biannually
Tier 2: RTO 24h, RPO 24h — backups + annual test
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: treating DR targets like SLOs brings the whole SRE machinery — measurement, alerting on drift, action items — to disaster recovery.

pitfalls: Architecture that can't meet the numbers

lessons.title: Failover drills as a practice
concepts: Drill the full cycle: failover AND failback. Failback is where the surprises live (replication direction, data reconciliation).
Drill in production during business hours with the team present. Staging drills prove tooling; production drills prove the system.
Scorecard every drill: RTO achieved, RPO achieved, surprises → action items. No scorecard, no proof.
Vary the scenario: fail over with a lagging replica, during a deploy, with a partial outage. Happy-path drills breed false confidence.

example.code:
Drill scorecard:
RTO target 15m → achieved 22m (gap: DNS caching)
RPO target 1m → achieved 40s
Surprises: failback script bug, stale runbook → 3 actions
Next drill: partial-outage scenario
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the scorecard quantifies belief vs reality; the DNS finding alone justified the drill. Varying scenarios prevents happy-path complacency.

lessons.title: Communication during disasters
concepts: Disasters need the incident comms discipline at larger scale: regular updates, impact-first, separate channels for responders/customers/execs/press.
Pre-write the templates: disaster declaration, customer notice, all-clear. Writing comms mid-disaster under pressure goes badly.
Designate spokespeople in advance: who talks to customers, who talks to execs, who talks to press. Confusion about voice = mixed messages.
Exercise comms in drills: the drill includes sending the (clearly marked drill) notifications. Untested comms fail when needed.

example.code:
Disaster comms plan:
- updates every 30 min (even 'no change')
- channels: #disaster-war, status page, exec bridge
- spokespeople: named in the plan
- templates pre-written and reviewed
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the plan removes decisions from the disaster — who talks, where, how often, saying what. Drilling it makes it muscle memory.

lessons.title: Ownership models
concepts: Every service has exactly one owning team: the team that gets paged, writes the runbooks, and defines the SLOs. Shared ownership = no ownership.
'You build it, you run it': the team shipping the service operates it. Handoffs to separate ops teams recreate the dev/ops divide.
Ownership includes the full lifecycle: design, deploy, monitor, incident response, decommission. Partial ownership creates orphans.
Make ownership visible: service catalog with owner, SLOs, runbooks, on-call. Invisible ownership can't be exercised.

example.code:
Service catalog entry:
service: checkout | owner: payments-team
SLOs: 99.95% success, p99 < 800ms
runbooks: linked | on-call: payments-rotation
health: budget 62% remaining
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the catalog entry is ownership made concrete — one team, named SLOs, linked runbooks, visible health. Gaps in the catalog are ownership gaps.

pitfalls: Build team vs run team split

lessons.title: Service handbooks
concepts: Every service gets a handbook: architecture, dependencies, SLOs, dashboards, alerts, runbooks, deployment, DR, and known issues. One page to start, grown over time.
The handbook is the on-call's brain: at 3am, the responder reads the handbook, not the original author's memory.
Keep it current: handbook review is part of the launch checklist and the quarterly service review. Stale handbooks are worse than none.
Template it org-wide: consistent handbooks let responders help with unfamiliar services — critical for escalation.

example.code:

# dashboards/alerts  # runbooks
# deploy + rollback  # DR plan

lessons.title: Runbook culture
concepts: Runbooks are executable where possible: scripts with dry-run, not prose about clicking. The runbook is automation's first draft.
Link runbooks from alerts: the page fires, the responder clicks, the commands are there. Unlinked runbooks don't exist at 3am.
Test runbooks quarterly: execute (or dry-run) every command. Drifted runbooks are incident-extenders.
Runbook coverage is a metric: % of alerts with linked, tested runbooks. Track it like SLO coverage.

example.code:

# [ ] tested this quarter

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the quality bar is checkable — coverage becomes a metric, not a hope. Tested runbooks turn 3am pages from puzzles into procedures.

lessons.title: Operational maturity assessments
concepts: Assess each service's operational maturity periodically: SLOs? runbooks? toil measured? DR tested? Score honestly — the gaps are the roadmap.
Use maturity to prioritize: low-maturity critical services get SRE engagement first. Data beats politics in prioritization.
Re-assess after engagements: the delta proves the work. Maturity trending up is the SRE org's KPI.
Publish the results (anonymized if needed): visibility creates healthy pressure. Nobody wants their service at the bottom.

lessons.title: Decommissioning: ownership to the end
concepts: Services need end-of-life ownership: migration plan, data handling, dependency notification, and a real shutdown date. Orphaned services are security and toil risks.
Announce early and repeat: consumers need time to migrate. The decommission plan is a project with an owner, not a hope.
Track the tail: services past their shutdown date get escalated. 'Temporary' services become permanent without enforcement.
Celebrate shutdowns: reclaiming the operational burden is a win. The team that decommissions well earns trust for the next build.

lessons.title: Negotiating SLOs with product
concepts: SLO negotiation is a business conversation: translate reliability into user impact and cost. '99.99% costs $X and slows feature Y' — let product choose with eyes open.
Bring data: user complaints vs latency percentiles, revenue impact of past incidents, cost curves per nine. Opinions lose to numbers.
Find the real requirement: product often asks for 99.99% meaning 'don't embarrass us'. The actual user need might be 99.9% + fast incident comms.
Document the agreement: SLO, budget policy, review date. Verbal SLOs evaporate at the first incident.

- proposal: 99.9% + comms SLA, review quarterly
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the prep turns 'we need five nines' into a cost/benefit discussion. The documented agreement prevents re-litigation every incident.

lessons.title: The reliability roadmap
concepts: The roadmap translates practices into quarters: Q1 SLO coverage, Q2 toil automation, Q3 chaos program — sequenced by dependency and pain.
Sequence by leverage: SLOs first (they govern everything), then alerting (detection), then toil (capacity), then advanced practices (chaos, multi-region).
Attach metrics to each milestone: '% services with SLOs: 30→80%', 'toil hours: 6→2'. Milestones without metrics are wishes.
Review quarterly with leadership: progress, blockers, reprioritization. The roadmap is a living commitment, not a annual slide.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the sequence builds the foundation first — chaos without SLOs is just breaking things. Metrics make each quarter checkable.

lessons.title: Leading cultural change
concepts: Culture changes through systems, not slogans: blameless postmortem templates, toil budgets, error-budget policies — practices that make the culture the easy path.
Find allies: the teams already doing it well become the examples. Mandates convert slower than visible success.
Measure the culture: postmortem action completion, toil trends, on-call NPS, safety survey scores. Cultural goals need metrics like any other.
Be patient and persistent: cultural change takes quarters. Celebrate intermediate wins; don't declare victory early.

3. expand via the practices (templates, policies)

lessons.title: Reliability reporting to leadership
concepts: Report reliability like a business metric: SLO compliance, budget health, incident trends, toil trajectory — monthly, one page, trends not snapshots.
Lead with user impact and business risk: 'checkout at 99.97% (target 99.95%), budget healthy' — not 'we closed 40 tickets'.
Include the asks: 'toil at 30%, need 2 quarters of automation focus' — reports without asks are just status.
Honesty builds the mandate: report the misses plainly with the fix. Sugarcoating destroys credibility exactly when you need it.

- asks: 1-2, specific

lessons.title: Hiring and growing SREs
concepts: Hire engineers who automate: coding interviews, systems design, and a 'tell me about toil you eliminated' story. Ops-only backgrounds struggle with the automation mandate.
Grow deliberately: pair juniors with seniors on incidents, rotate postmortem facilitation, fund conference and writing time. SRE judgment is apprenticeship-shaped.
Retain with the ladder: SRE needs promotion paths to senior+ that don't require leaving for product teams. Losing automators to feature work is the tax on a broken ladder.
Diversity of background matters: SRE benefits from varied systems experience — different outages seen, different patterns recognized.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the loop selects for the actual job — automating operations and practicing reliability — not for trivia. The practices deep-dive is the differentiator.

lessons.title: Capstone part 2: the improvement roadmap
concepts: Deliverable 2: a 4-quarter improvement roadmap sequenced by leverage — SLOs and alerting first, toil and culture next, advanced practices last.
Each roadmap item: the practice gap, the proposed change, the metric it moves, the owner, and the quarter. No metric, no roadmap slot.
Include quick wins: 2-3 items shippable in 30 days (alert tuning, runbook linking, postmortem template) to build momentum and credibility.

lessons.title: Capstone part 3: present and defend

Ship the package: report, roadmap, slides, and an appendix of artifacts. A portfolio artifact that proves you can assess and lead, not just recite.

simulations.title: The 14x burn
simulations.brief: The checkout SLO is 99.9% over 30 days. The burn-rate alert fired: 2% of the error budget consumed in 1 hour. Work the response.

steps.symptom: Fast-burn alert: 2% of the monthly error budget gone in one hour. Burn rate 14.4x.
evidence: SLO: checkout 99.9% / 30d. Error budget: 43.2 min/month. Consumed in last 1h: 2%. Burn rate: 14.4x (fast burn).
options: The deploy at 14:02 correlates exactly with the burn — roll back the timeout change first
Add more checkout pods
The SLO window is misconfigured
Increase the error budget
steps.explain: A 14x burn rate starting right after a config change is a smoking gun. The 5s timeout is likely too aggressive; the correct move is rollback first, then investigate.

steps.symptom: Burn confirmed tied to the deploy. What is the immediate action?
evidence: 14:21 rollback to v2.14.0 complete. Burn rate falling: 14.4x -> 1.2x.
options: Roll back to v2.14.0 and watch the burn rate
Page the whole org immediately
Delete the SLO to stop the alert
Wait for the budget to exhaust
steps.explain: Rollback stops the bleeding because it reverses the suspected cause. Postmortems come after the budget stops burning, never during.

steps.symptom: Rollback worked. How do you protect the recovery?
evidence: While error budget burn > 2x: freeze non-urgent deploys to the affected service.
options: Freeze non-urgent checkout deploys until burn normalizes, then postmortem
Immediately redeploy v2.14.1 with a fix
Blame the deploy author in the incident channel
Lower the SLO to 99% so the alert clears
steps.explain: Error budgets are policy, not just math: while burning fast, freeze risky changes so the recovery is not undone by the next deploy.

simulations.debrief: Burn rate turns an SLO into an operational signal: fast burn pages, slow burn tickets. Respond proportional to the burn, and freeze risky changes while the budget bleeds.

simulations.title: CPU is not an SLI
simulations.brief: The team's 'reliability dashboard' tracks CPU, memory, and disk across the fleet — all green. Meanwhile the checkout SLO burned 30% of budget last week unnoticed. Rebuild the measurement.

steps.symptom: Fleet dashboard all green. Checkout error budget: 30% consumed in a week. Nobody noticed.
evidence: CPU avg 45%, memory 60%, disk 50% — all green thresholds.
Checkout: 99.9% target, actual 99.62% this week. Budget consumed: 30%. No alert fired.
options: Define SLIs on what users experience — success rate and latency percentiles — and alert on budget burn, not resource thresholds
Lower the CPU thresholds so the dashboard turns red more often
The SLO must be wrong — 99.62% is basically 99.9%
Add more resource metrics to the dashboard
steps.explain: SLIs measure what users experience: success rate, latency percentiles, freshness. Resource metrics inform capacity; they are not SLIs. A green fleet dashboard with a burning error budget is measuring the wrong thing.

steps.symptom: The team defines a checkout success-rate SLI. Debate: should it include 4xx errors?
evidence: Checkout requests: 2% 4xx (user errors: bad cards, bad addresses), 0.4% 5xx (our failures).
options: Exclude user-caused 4xx from the SLI: the SLI measures the system's reliability, not user mistakes — but track 4xx separately for product insight
Count everything — simpler and stricter
Exclude all 4xx and 5xx — only count timeouts
SLIs shouldn't use error rates at all
steps.explain: The SLI should reflect what the system owes the user: successful handling of valid requests. User errors (bad cards) are product signal, not reliability signal — mixing them punishes the SLI for user behavior and hides real regressions.

steps.symptom: SLI defined and burning properly. Now: what does the team do when the budget is exhausted?
evidence: Budget exhausted with 9 days left in the window. Feature freeze proposed.
'We can't stop shipping — the roadmap is committed.'
options: Honor the budget contract: reliability work takes priority until the budget recovers — the trade-off was negotiated in advance
Keep shipping — roadmaps outrank budgets
Lower the SLO to restore budget instantly
Borrow budget from next month
steps.explain: The error budget is the allowed unreliability, and the trade-off is negotiated in advance, not during the incident: budget remaining ships fast, budget exhausted means reliability work first. Overriding it 'just this once' teaches the org the budget is decorative.

simulations.debrief: Measure what users feel, alert on budget burn, and honor the budget contract. Resource dashboards inform capacity planning — they are not reliability instrumentation.

simulations.title: Who runs the incident
simulations.brief: Checkout is down. Seven engineers are in the channel, all debugging different theories, nobody talking to customers. The incident has no structure. Impose it.

steps.symptom: 7 engineers debugging in parallel, 0 coordination, 0 customer communication. 25 minutes in.
evidence: 7 threads: DNS theory, deploy theory, DB theory, 'works for me', ... No decisions.
Status page: last updated 3 days ago. Support: 'Customers are asking us.'
options: Declare the incident and assign roles: commander, comms, ops — coordination first, debugging second
Let the 7 theories race — the fastest debugger wins
Everyone stop and wait for the most senior engineer
The incident will resolve itself once someone finds it
steps.explain: Incident response is a coordination discipline first: declare, assign roles (commander, comms, ops), run a rhythm, communicate outward. Seven parallel theories with no coordination is slower than one coordinated investigation.

steps.symptom: Roles assigned. The commander is also deep in the database logs.
evidence: Commander: also running queries. Comms: silent. Ops: waiting for direction.
40 minutes in. No customer update yet.
options: The commander commands: step out of the logs, run the rhythm, and get the comms role publishing updates
The commander should debug — they're the best engineer
Disband the roles — they slow things down
Comms can wait until the fix is found
steps.explain: The commander's job is the incident, not the bug: maintaining the rhythm, tracking theories, and ensuring comms publishes outward. A commander with their head in logs is an incident with no one flying the plane.

steps.symptom: Incident resolved. The proposed postmortem title: 'Engineer error: wrong config deployed.'
evidence: Root cause: 'Engineer deployed wrong config.' Action: 'Be more careful.'
Same config path caused 2 prior incidents. No guardrails added either time.
options: Rewrite it blameless: the human error is the starting point — the system allowed the wrong config to deploy unchecked
The title is accurate — accountability matters
Skip the postmortem — the fix is deployed
Punish the engineer to set an example
steps.explain: Blameless postmortems fix systems, not people — human error is the starting point, never the root cause. Twice before, the same path burned; 'be more careful' fixed nothing. The action item is the guardrail that makes the error impossible.

simulations.debrief: Incidents need declared roles and a commander who coordinates instead of debugging; postmortems need blameless system fixes. Structure is what turns chaos into learning.

simulations.title: The toil trap
simulations.brief: The SRE team spends 70% of its time on manual ticket-driven ops work: password resets, manual deploys, hand-run reports. Reliability projects never start. Break the cycle.

steps.symptom: SRE time audit: 70% manual ops tickets, 20% meetings, 10% project work. Toil is the job.
evidence: Top tickets: password resets (manual), deploy approvals (manual), weekly reports (hand-built).
Reliability roadmap: 0 items started in 2 quarters.
options: Cap the toil and automate it away in priority order — toil is manual, repetitive, automatable work with no enduring value
Hire 3 more SREs to handle the ticket load
Toil is the job — SRE means ops
Stop measuring — the numbers are demoralizing
steps.explain: Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable work with no enduring value. Cap it, then automate it away — hiring into toil just scales the toil. Every hire should reduce toil, not absorb it.

steps.symptom: The team automates password resets. Now deploy approvals: 'too risky to automate.'
evidence: Manual deploy approvals: 40/week, ~2 min each, rubber-stamped 99% of the time.
'What if the automation approves a bad deploy?'
options: Automate the checks the humans actually perform, keep the human gate for genuine judgment calls — rubber-stamping is toil wearing a gate costume
Keep manual approvals — the risk is real
Remove approvals entirely — velocity first
Make approvals require two humans for safety
steps.explain: A 99%-rubber-stamped approval is toil, not safety: automate the verifiable checks (tests green, scans clean, canary healthy) and reserve human judgment for the ambiguous cases. The gate should check things, not perform diligence theater.

steps.symptom: Toil down to 30%. Leadership asks the team to absorb another service's on-call 'since you have capacity now.'
evidence: 'You've automated so well — take the payments on-call too.'
New on-call load would return toil+interrupt time to 65%.
options: Defend the reclaimed capacity for reliability work — the automation dividend funds the roadmap, not new toil
Accept — the team proved it can handle load
Accept but hire one more person
Refuse all new work forever
steps.explain: The automation dividend belongs to reliability work — that's the entire point of eliminating toil. Absorbing new operational load with it just refills the toil bucket. Sustainable teams convert toil reduction into engineering time, visibly.

simulations.debrief: Toil is the enemy of reliability work: cap it, automate the automatable, keep humans for judgment — and defend the freed capacity for the roadmap. Hiring into toil scales the toil.

simulations.title: The slow burn nobody ticketed
simulations.brief: The fast-burn page works. But the slow-burn alert fires tickets that sit for weeks — the search API has been at 6x burn for a month, and the budget will exhaust quietly. Make slow burn actionable.

steps.symptom: Slow-burn alert (6x over 6h/30m windows) has filed 11 tickets in a month. All still open. Budget 70% consumed.
evidence: 11 slow-burn tickets, 0 closed, oldest 28 days. Assignees: various, none active.
Search API burn: steady 6x for 30 days. Projection: budget exhausted in 12 days.
options: Treat slow-burn tickets as real work: triage them into the sprint with the burn data attached — slow burn is still burn
Slow burn isn't urgent — that's why it's a ticket
Close the tickets — the fast-burn alert will catch real problems
Raise the slow-burn threshold so fewer tickets file
steps.explain: Burn-rate alerting ties pages to the budget: fast-burn pages a human; slow-burn files a ticket — but the ticket must be worked. A month of ignored 6x burn is the budget exhausting in slow motion while everyone watches the fast-burn pager.

steps.symptom: The team triages the tickets: the search degradation comes from an unindexed query pattern growing with data volume.
evidence: Slow queries: full-scan on the events table, growing linearly with data.
Data volume: +8%/month. Query cost: +8%/month. Budget burn: accelerating.
options: Fix the query pattern (index, pagination, caching) — slow burn from growth compounds, so the fix pays monthly dividends
It's only slow burn — monitor it
Add database capacity to absorb the growth
The burn will stabilize on its own
steps.explain: Slow-burn causes are often growth-coupled: the unindexed query gets 8% more expensive every month, so the burn accelerates. Fixing the pattern pays compounding dividends; adding capacity just moves the exhaustion date.

steps.symptom: Fixed. Now the team debates whether slow-burn alerts are worth keeping at all.
evidence: 'Fast burn caught every real incident. Slow burn just made tickets.'
This incident: caught only by slow burn, 30 days before exhaustion.
options: Keep both: fast burn pages for urgency, slow burn tickets for the important-but-not-urgent — this incident proves the pair
Drop slow burn — fast burn is sufficient
Make slow burn page too — everything urgent
Alerting is overhead — rely on dashboards
steps.explain: Multiwindow burn-rate alerting distinguishes urgency: fast burn (14.4x over 1h/5m) pages now; slow burn (6x over 6h/30m) tickets the important-but-not-urgent. This incident existed only in the slow window — dropping it blinds you to the quiet exhaustions.

simulations.debrief: Slow burn is still burn: ticket it, work it, fix the growth-coupled causes — and keep the multiwindow pair. Fast burn saves the night; slow burn saves the quarter.
